(p-4020) Surah al-Kahf

It is also called Surat Ashab al-Kahf (the Surah of the Companions of the Cave). Al-Mahayimi said: It was named thus because it includes the story of its companions, which comprises the benefits of faith in God: complete security from enemies, complete independence from things, and wondrous marvels (karamat, miraculous gifts granted to the righteous). This is among the greatest aims of the Qur'an. It is Meccan, though it has been said that its first part up to His saying ﴿barren land﴾ [al-Kahf: 8], and His saying ﴿And keep yourself patient﴾ [al-Kahf: 28] and the verse, and ﴿Indeed, those who have believed﴾ [al-Kahf: 107] to the end of the surah, are Medinan.

Al-Dani chose that it is entirely Meccan. Its number of verses is one hundred and ten. Many hadiths have been related concerning its virtues, which Al-Hafiz Ibn Kathir and others have cited.

(p-4021) In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

The discussion on the interpretation of His, the Exalted's, saying:

[1] ﴿Praise be to God, who has sent down to His servant the Book and has not made in it any crookedness﴾

﴿Praise be to God, who has sent down to His servant the Book﴾: We have previously mentioned that surahs are often opened and closed with praise, as an indication that He is the One praised in every state: ﴿To Him belongs praise in the first and the last﴾ [al-Qasas: 70], and as a teaching to the servants of the etiquette of beginning every important matter with praise and concluding it with praise. This is by extolling God, blessed and exalted, for His great blessings and supreme favors. In choosing the sending down of the revelation from among all His other sublime attributes, there is an alert that it is the greatest of His bounties, for it is the guide to what contains the perfection of the servants, and the caller to what organizes the welfare of this life and the Hereafter. Nothing in its meaning resembles it. In mentioning the Messenger (ﷺ) with the title of servanthood, there is an alert to the greatness of the one sent down and the one to whom it was sent down, as indicated by the exclusive possessive construction, as was previously mentioned in Surat al-Isra'. It also signals that it is the station of the Messenger to be a servant of the One who sent him, unlike what the Christians claimed concerning Jesus, peace be upon him. The definiteness of "the Book" is for previous reference, i.e., the complete Book, free from needing description as complete, known as such among books, deserving that the name "Book" be exclusively applied to it. It refers to the entire Qur'an, or to all that was sent down at that time. Its being placed after the prepositional phrase, although its proper place is before it, is so that His, glory be to Him, saying ﴿and has not made in it any crookedness﴾ may be joined to it, meaning: not any crookedness, by disorder in its composition or contradiction in its meanings, or deviation and departure from calling to the truth. Rather, He made it a remover of crookedness; since He made it:

[p-4022] On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[2] ﴿Upright, to warn of severe punishment from Him, and to give good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds that they shall have a goodly reward﴾ [3] ﴿abiding therein forever﴾ [al-Kahf: 2–3]

﴿Upright﴾ means: upright in managing the welfare of the servants and in the laws (shara'i') they cannot do without. This is a description of it as perfecting them, after the description of it as perfect in itself. Or, it means upright over the earlier Scriptures, watching over them (muhayminan 'alayha). Or, it means extremely straight and balanced, so that it confirms what the negation of crookedness indicates, along with conveying that this is one of its essential, inherent attributes, as the form of the word indicates. Its grammatical accusative (intisab) is by an implied verb whose estimate is "He made it," as we have mentioned, on the basis that it is a resumed independent clause. There are other possibilities.

Note (tanbih):

Al-Qashani held that the pronoun in "lahu" (to Him) and what follows refers to "His servant" (in His words "upon His servant"). He said: meaning, He did not make crookedness and deviation for His servant. He made him upright, meaning straight, as he was commanded in His words: ﴿So be upright as you have been commanded﴾ [Hud: 112]; or upright in managing the affairs and guidance of the servants, since perfecting others follows from perfection. For when he, upon him be peace and blessings, had finished setting himself straight and purifying himself, the souls of his community were placed in the position of his own soul, so he was commanded to set them straight and purify them. For this reason Abraham, peace be upon him, was called an ummah. This uprightness, meaning standing to guide people, falls within the straightness that he was in reality commanded to, end of quote.

The first possibility is more apparent.

His exalted words ﴿to warn of a severe punishment from Him﴾ mean: to warn whoever opposes him and does not believe in him of a severe punishment, immediate or deferred. "Ba's" (bas) means subjugation and punishment. He specified it with His words ﴿from Him﴾ to indicate its increased terror, and for this reason He magnified it by indefiniteness. It is connected either to "anzala" (He sent down) or to the operator of "qayyiman" (upright). ﴿And to give good tidings [p-4023] to the believers﴾ means: by it. Al-Qashani said: meaning the monotheists, because they stand in opposition to the polytheists who said, "God has taken a son." His exalted words ﴿who do righteous deeds﴾ mean: of good things and virtues. ﴿That for them﴾ means: that for them, in exchange for their faith and their aforementioned deeds, ﴿is a goodly reward﴾, which is Paradise. ﴿Abiding therein forever﴾ [al-Kahf: 3].

[p-4022] On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[2] ﴿Upright, to warn of severe punishment from Him, and to give good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds that they shall have a goodly reward﴾ [3] ﴿abiding therein forever﴾ [al-Kahf: 2–3]

The commentary on His words, exalted is He:

[4] ﴿And warn those who say, "Allah has taken a son."﴾

﴿And warn those who say, "Allah has taken a son."﴾ They are the polytheists of the Arabs, in their saying that the angels are the daughters of Allah, and the Christians, in their claim that the Messiah is the son of Allah. He singled them out for mention and repeated the warning as attached to them, in order to magnify their disbelief. And the omission of applying the relative clause to the antecedent, as He did in His words, ﴿and give good tidings to the believers﴾ [al-Kahf: 2], serves as an indication that what falls within the scope of the relative clause (the saying) is sufficient, in disbelief, in its most hideous form.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[5] ﴿They have no knowledge of it, nor did their fathers. Grave is the word that comes out of their mouths. They say nothing but a lie.﴾

﴿They have no knowledge of it, nor did their fathers.﴾ That is: they have no knowledge concerning the child, or taking one, or the saying, [none] at all. Rather, it issues only from extreme ignorance, false imagining, and blind imitation of their fathers, not from knowledge of certainty and conviction. This is supported by His words: ﴿Grave is the word﴾, that is, how great a word it is, ﴿that comes out of their mouths﴾. This is because a child is impossible and has no meaning. For certain knowledge bears witness that the Necessary Existence is singular in its essence, and that contingent existence cannot be like it. The child is one who resembles his father in kind and is equal to him in power. The clause ﴿that comes out of their mouths﴾ is a description of "word" (kalimah), conveying the magnification of their audacity in uttering it from their mouths. Al-Shihab said: "Because the meaning is: its coming out is great", that is, its ugliness and repulsiveness are magnified by the mere uttering of it. So what of believing it? ﴿They say nothing but a lie﴾, that is, a saying that is a lie, which can hardly fall within the realm of truth at all. This is because definitive proof and the intuitive sense agree on its impossibility.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 18, verse 6:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[6] ﴿So perhaps you would kill yourself with grief over them, if they do not believe in this discourse, out of sorrow.﴾

﴿So perhaps you would kill yourself﴾ means: destroying yourself, ﴿with grief over them, if they do not believe in this discourse﴾, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿out of sorrow﴾, meaning: so that you grieve over their turning away and their aversion from it. Or: grieving over them. Al-asaf is the excess of sorrow and anger. In al-'Inayah, "la'alla" (perhaps) expresses hope (tarajji), which is the desire for something to occur or the apprehension of it. Here it is a metaphor (isti'arah), meaning: you have reached a state in which people expect this of you, because of what is observed of your grief over their not believing. In the noble composition there is a figurative metaphor (isti'arah tamthiliyyah), by likening his condition with them, when they have turned away, while he is grieved over their lack of guidance, to the condition of one whose beloved ones have departed from him, so he resolves to kill himself, or nearly perishes from longing for them and anguish over their traces. The secret of this, as al-Qashani said, is that compassion for God's creation and mercy toward them are among the necessary consequences and fruits of the love of God. Since he, may God bless him and grant him peace, was the beloved of God, and among the necessary consequences of his being beloved is his love for God, in accordance with His saying: ﴿He loves them and they love Him﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 54], and whenever his love for the Truth is stronger, his compassion and mercy toward His creation are greater, because compassion for them is the shadow of his love for God and the most intense of his tenderness toward them, for they are like his children and his relatives, indeed like his limbs and members in true witnessing. Therefore he exceeded in grieving over them, to the point that he nearly destroyed himself. And His saying, exalted is He:

The Word of Allah Most High concerning His saying:

[7] ﴿Indeed, We have made what is on the earth an adornment for it, that We may test them as to which of them is best in deed.﴾

﴿Indeed, We have made what is on the earth﴾, i.e., of animals, plants, and minerals, ﴿an adornment for it, that We may test them as to which of them is best in deed﴾, i.e., that it may become manifest which of them is most subduing of its desires and its incitements, most disobedient to its whims, meaning My pleasure, and most capable of opposing it in order to agree with Me.

(p-4025) The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[8] ﴿And indeed We will make that which is upon it a barren, desolate ground.﴾

﴿And indeed We will make that which is upon it a barren, desolate ground.﴾ That is: dust, level, with no vegetation in it, after it had been delighting the beholders, with nothing in it varying, hills and valleys. That is: We will annihilate it and what is upon it, and We will not care. In the verse there is consolation for him, may the blessings of Allah be upon him. It is as if it were said: Do not grieve over them, for it is no concern of yours that they should all perish, because We bring all the means from non-existence into existence for the sake of trial, then We annihilate them, with no injustice and no deficiency. Or: do not grieve, for We will annihilate that and requite them according to their deeds. And His saying, exalted is He:

The discussion concerning the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[9] ﴿Or do you think that the companions of the cave and the inscription were among Our signs as a marvel?﴾

﴿Or do you think that the companions of the cave and the inscription were among Our signs as a marvel?﴾ That is: a sign possessing wonder, by omitting a modifier (ḥadhf muḍāf). Or it is a description with the verbal noun (maṣdar) for emphasis (mubālaghah), and ﴿among Our signs﴾ is a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of it. And ﴿am﴾ (or) is for the interrogation of affirmation (al-istifhām al-taqrīrī) with the meaning of the hamzah (the interrogative particle alif). That is: they are, among Our signs, a wondrous sign. He took it as a disjunctive (munqaṭi'ah) and presumed to be bi-bal (rather) and the hamzah, with the interrogation being for denial, i.e., the denial of their supposition that they were a wondrous sign in comparison with His great signs, is far-fetched. Because the context of the noble composition, I mean its presentation in detail and its being highlighted, is only for affirming the wonder at them. And (al-Kahf) is the wide cave in the mountain. And (al-Raqīm) is the name of their dog. It was said it is a tablet (lawḥ raqīm) in which their account was written, and it was placed at the entrance of the cave. It was said it is the mountain or the valley; these are opinions.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 18, verse 10:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[10] ﴿When the youths sought refuge in the cave, they said: "Our Lord, grant us mercy from Yourself and facilitate for us a right course in our affair."﴾

﴿When the youths sought refuge in the cave﴾ i.e., out of fear of the king's harm for abandoning the worship of idols and sacrificing to them. Choosing the explicit noun over the pronoun (al-izhar 'ala al-idmar, the explicit noun instead of the pronoun) serves to affirm their state by giving precedence to the side of God over the side of their desires during their youth. ﴿They said: "Our Lord"﴾ i.e., the One who nurtured us with the blessing of preferring His side over the side of our own souls. ﴿Grant us mercy from Yourself﴾ i.e., from Your treasuries, which are forgiveness, provision and security from enemies. ﴿And facilitate for us our affair﴾ which is choosing the cave to separate ourselves from the disbelievers. ﴿A right course﴾ which is Your affirmation of oneness and Your worship.

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, the Exalted:

[11] ﴿So We struck over their ears in the cave for a number of years﴾.

﴿So We struck over their ears in the cave for a number of years﴾: that is, We made them sleep a heavy sleep, such that neither the whistle of the One Who is Aware (al-Khabir) nor the call of the caller can rouse them; "in the cave for a number of years, countable," that is, many, or limited in number. Al-Shihab said: "Darabna (We struck) is used metaphorically, by way of a subordinate metaphor (isti'ara tab'iyya), for the meaning of 'We made them sleep,' a sleep from which they cannot be awakened by shouting, because the sleeper is roused through his hearing. It is either derived from 'I locked the door' (darabtu al-qufl 'ala al-bab) or from 'I drew the tent over its occupant' (darabtu al-khiba' 'ala sakinihi), being likened, in their being deeply absorbed in sleep so that no caller can wake them, to one who is behind barriers that prevent sounds from reaching him." It has also been said that it is a metaphor of the representative kind (isti'ara tamthiliyya).

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[12] ﴿Then We roused them, that We might know which of the two parties was more precise in computing the time they had remained.﴾

﴿Then We roused them﴾, i.e., We awoke them with an awakening resembling the raising of the dead. ﴿that We might know which of the two parties was more precise in computing the time they had remained﴾, i.e., that We might know in actual fact what We already knew would occur. The two parties differed concerning the length of their stay, and the one that was more exact in computing (ahsa), i.e., in comprehending and precisely determining the full extent of the period they had remained, so that they would know the measure of what God had preserved them through, without food or drink, and had kept them safe from their enemy. Thus their right guidance would be complete in giving thanks to Him, and it would be a sign for them that moves them to worship Him.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 18, verse 13:

Al-Qawl fi ta'wil qawlihi ta'ala (Discussion on the interpretation of His Exalted saying):

[13] ﴿We relate to you their story in truth. Indeed, they were youths who believed in their Lord, and We increased them in guidance.﴾

﴿We relate to you their story in truth﴾ begins the completion of the detailed exposition of their account. "Truth" (al-haqq) is the matter that corresponds to reality. ﴿Indeed, they were youths who believed in their Lord﴾, i.e., in His oneness, with a certain faith, grounded in knowledge, by way of reasoning, while their people were agreed upon polytheism. ﴿And We increased them in guidance﴾, i.e., by giving preponderance to the side of God over the side of their own souls. Ibn Kathir said: The youths, who are the young men, are more receptive to the truth and better guided to the path than the elders who have become obstinate and immersed in the religion of falsehood. For this reason most of those who responded to God Most High and His Messenger (ﷺ) were young. As for the general body of the elders of Quraysh, they persisted in their misguidance, and only a few of them embraced Islam. Likewise, God Most High informed us concerning the People of the Cave that they were young men. Various confused narrations have been related about these youths. The most reliable of them is that a man came to their city calling to faith in God Most High and to what 'Isa (peace be upon him) had brought, being of the Hawariyyun (the disciples) in lineage. The youths mentioned responded to this, renounced the idolatry in which their people were, and fled with their religion, fearing that their king would tempt them away from their religion or kill them. They hid from him in the cave and withdrew there, worshipping God Most High alone. Then it is related that the king sought them. It was said: they entered this cave. Their people said: We do not want for them any punishment or torment worse than that we wall up this cave over them. So they built it over them and then sealed it. Then God sent over them a king upon the religion of 'Isa, and he removed that structure which had been sealed over them. Some of them said to others: ﴿How long have you remained?﴾ They said: ﴿We have remained a day or part of a day﴾ [al-Kahf: 19], until: ﴿So send one of you with this silver of yours to the city﴾ [al-Kahf: 19]. The silver of that era bore the coinage of their rulers. They sent one of them to bring them food. When he went out, he saw at the entrance of the cave something that he disapproved of, and he wanted to return. Then he proceeded until he entered the city, and he disowned what he had seen. Then he took out a dirham, and they looked at it and disapproved of it, and they disapproved of the dirham as well. They said: From where do you have this? This is silver from a different age.

They gathered around him asking him, and did not cease with him until they took him to their king. He informed him of his affair, and they rejoiced at him and at his companions. It was said to him: Go, show us your companions. He went, and they went with him so that he might show them. He entered before the people and struck upon their ears, and ﴿those who prevailed over their affair said: We will surely take over them a place of worship﴾ [al-Kahf: 21]. This is what Ibn Jarir reported first, and it is sufficient in place of others.

We shall mention at the end of their account what the People of the Book, the Christians, say about their affair.

It has been said that they were in a city called (Tarsus), among the districts of Tripoli of Syria. In it, on a mountain, there are ancient remains, which its people claim by inherited assertion to belong to the People of the Cave. And God knows best.

Then Allah, exalted is He, explained their steadfastness in opposing their people, and their leaving their city and the comfortable life they had enjoyed in it, by His saying:

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[14] ﴿And We made their hearts firm when they stood up and said: "Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth. We shall never call upon any god besides Him. We would have then uttered an enormity."﴾

﴿And We made their hearts firm﴾: that is, We strengthened them with patience in striving (mujahadah). We encouraged them to fight Satan, to flee with their religion to some caves, to oppose the self (nafs), to abandon worldly pleasures and bodily delights, and to uphold the word of monotheism (kalimat al-tawhid). It has also been said: We emboldened them to uphold the word of monotheism, to manifest the upright religion, and to call to the truth in the presence of their tyrannical king. This is based on His saying: ﴿when they stood up﴾, that is, before him, not caring about him. "Idh" (when) is an adverbial clause (zarf) governed by "rabatna" (We made firm).

Al-Shihab said: The "rabt" (binding) upon the heart is a metaphor (majaz) for the literal meaning of rabt, which is tightening (al-shadd). That is, it is a figurative borrowing from it, as one says "rabit al-ja'ash" (one whose heart is bound, i.e., steadfast). This is because anxiety and fear cause the heart to be displaced from its place, as Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿And the hearts will reach the throats﴾ [al-Ahzab: 10]. So the heart that is calmed about a matter is likened to an animal tied in a place. "Rabat" is transitive by itself, but it is made to take "ʿalā" (upon) because it has been treated as intransitive (lazim). ﴿Then they said: "Our Lord"﴾, the One whom we worship, ﴿is the Lord of the heavens and the earth﴾, such that every object of worship other than Him comes under His lordship. ﴿We shall never call upon﴾, that is, worship, ﴿any god besides Him. We would have then uttered an enormity﴾, that is, something far from the truth and grossly excessive in wrongdoing.

The discussion of the words of His exalted saying:

[15] ﴿These, our people, have taken besides Him gods. Why do they not bring for them a clear authority? Who then is more unjust than one who invents against Allah a lie?﴾

﴿These, our people, have taken besides Him gods﴾: they made or carved for them gods, which indicates that they worshipped them. In the demonstrative there is belittlement of them. ﴿Why do they not bring for them﴾: i.e., for their worship, or their divinity, or their influence. ﴿a clear authority﴾: i.e., a manifest proof and an evident demonstration, for religion is not taken except by it. Al-Qashani said: this is evidence for the corruption of blind imitation (taqlid), and a rebuke that establishing proof for the divinity of other than Allah, and for its influence and existence, is impossible. As He said: ﴿They are but names you have named, you and your fathers, for which Allah has sent down no authority﴾ [al-Najm: 23], i.e., names without things named, because they are nothing. ﴿Who then is more unjust than one who invents against Allah a lie﴾: i.e., there is no equal to him in injustice and disbelief. It is an indication that they cannot produce any proof. They are thus unjust with regard to the right of Allah, for their inventing against Him that in His exalted rank there are partners who share it with Him. Then some of them addressed others, saying:

The Explanation of His Words, exalted is He:

[16] ﴿And when you withdraw from them and what they worship, except Allah, then take refuge in the cave; your Lord will spread out for you of His mercy and will prepare for you a means of ease in your affair.﴾

﴿And when you withdraw from them and what they worship, except Allah, then take refuge in the cave﴾ That is: and when you withdraw from the people, by abandoning following them, because of the extreme of their wrongdoing, which makes their hatred necessary; and you withdraw from their deities other than Allah, for they worshipped them either openly or within their worship of Him. "Then take refuge in the cave," which they cannot see you in, so they will not harm you, and do not fear dwelling in it because of the lack of food and drink. For when you seek refuge in Allah, after you have called upon Him, [He will do so] by spreading mercy and preparing right guidance: ﴿your Lord will spread out for you of His mercy﴾, that is, that which will suffice you instead of food and drink, through angelic supports and holy confirmations. ﴿And will prepare for you a means of ease in your affair﴾, which is choosing His side over yours: ﴿a means of ease﴾, that is, that by which you benefit. Al-Mahayimi said: "He will be gentle with your souls, giving them of the delights of His worship what makes them forget all other delights, whereas their delights were never free of harm, while these are free of all harms. Their certainty of this is due to the purity of their conviction and the strength of their trust in the bounty of Allah, exalted is He."

Caution:

Some people claimed that the verse indicates the legitimacy and recommendation of seclusion absolutely. This is an error. Rather, it points to following the example of the People of the Cave in withdrawing when a person is persecuted in his religion and is compelled to shirk. Among those who rejected using this verse as evidence for preferring seclusion is the Imam al-Ghazali, where he said in his (Ihya'): "The People of the Cave did not withdraw from one another, and they were believers; rather they withdrew from the disbelievers." That is: there is no doubt about its legitimacy as a means of fleeing from trials.

As for al-Suyuti's statement in (al-Iklil): "The verse contains the legitimacy of seclusion, fleeing from oppressors, and dwelling in caves and mountains when times become corrupt," it is a general statement that requires detailing. And which era has been free of corruption? The context of the verse concerns persecution alone, so understand this and do not exaggerate. And His words, exalted is He:

The Discussion on the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[17] ﴿And you would see the sun, when it rose, inclining away from their cave to the right, and when it set, passing them on the left, while they were in a spacious place within it. That is among the signs of Allah. Whoever Allah guides is the one rightly guided; but for whomever He sends astray, you will never find for him a protecting guardian who could guide him.﴾

﴿And you would see the sun when it rose﴾ i.e., it ascended at its rising. ﴿Inclining﴾ i.e., turning aside. ﴿Away from their cave﴾ i.e., from its entrance. ﴿To the right﴾ i.e., the right side of the cave. ﴿And when it set﴾ i.e., descended toward setting. ﴿Passing them on the left﴾ i.e., cutting across them and deviating from the direction of their heads toward the north side. ﴿While they were in a spacious place within it﴾ i.e., an expanse within the cave where air reaches them from every side without the harm of the sun. The verse indicates that the entrance of that cave faced the north. When the sun rose, it was on the right of the cave, and when it set, it was on its left. Thus its rays fall on both its sides, purifying its stagnancy and balancing its air, without falling on them and harming them.

Al-Shihab said: "Taqriduhum" is from the qarḍ (cutting) meaning, i.e., it cut off contact with them so that their bodies would not become dusty. The view of al-Farisi that it is from qarḍ al-darahim (lending of dirhams), meaning that it gives them some of its warmth and then quickly disappears, like a loan that is returned, is rejected, because no triliteral form of it has been heard.

In (al-Rawḍ al-Anf), "taqriduhum" is a metaphor for "ta'dilu bihim" (turns away from them). It was also said: it passes beyond them somewhat, from (al-qarḍ), which is cutting, i.e., it cuts through what lies there of the land.

And His words, Exalted is He: ﴿That is among the signs of Allah﴾ i.e., their being guided to this cave in which He made them alive, with the rays of the sun and the wind entering upon them in it so that their bodies might remain, a sign from His signs that indicates His care and His granting of success to the sincere.

﴿Whomever Allah guides﴾ i.e., to the truth by granting him success in it: ﴿he is the one rightly guided; and whomever He sends astray﴾ i.e., He creates misguidance in him by turning his choice toward it: ﴿you will never find for him a protecting guardian﴾ i.e., a helper who takes charge of his affair and thus protects him from misguidance: ﴿who could guide him﴾ i.e., guide him to what has been mentioned.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted Is He:

[18] ﴿And you would think them awake, while they are asleep. And We turn them to the right and to the left, and their dog stretches out its forelegs at the threshold. If you had looked upon them, you would have turned from them in flight, and you would have been filled with dread of them.﴾

(p-4032) ﴿And you would think them awake, while they are asleep﴾ is an address to every listener. That is: you would suppose them, O addressee, to be awake because their eyes are open, while they are asleep, sunk deep in sleep such that a sound does not rouse them. Ibn Kathir said: Some of the people of knowledge have mentioned that when God struck their ears with sleep, their eyes did not close, lest decay quickly reach them; and when they remain open to the air, they last longer. It has been related of the wolf that it sleeps by closing one eye and opening the other, then opening this one and closing that one while still asleep, as the poet said:

"He sleeps with one of his eyelids, and with the other he guards against calamities; he is awake and asleep at once."

And ﴿awake﴾ (aqẓan) is the plural of yaqiẓ and yaqẓān. And ﴿asleep﴾ (ruqūd) is the plural of rāqid. As for what has been said, that it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) used in the sense of the agent, applying equally to the singular and the plural, like rukūʿ and quʿūd, because fāʿil is not pluralized as fuʿūl, this is rejected by what the grammarians have stated, as declared in (al-Mufaḍḍal) and (al-Tashīl).

﴿And We turn them﴾, that is, during their sleep, ﴿to the right and to the left﴾, that is, lest the earth consume their bodies. ﴿And their dog stretches out its forelegs at the threshold﴾, that is, at the courtyard of the cave or its door. Their blessing has encompassed their dog: it was afflicted by what afflicted them of sleep in that state. Ibn Kathir said: This is the benefit of companionship with the righteous, for this dog came to have a mention, a report, and a standing. It has been said that it was a hunting dog belonging to them, and this is the more likely. People have differed about its color in various opinions, which have no substance, no benefit, no proof, and no need for them. Indeed, they are among the things forbidden, for their basis is conjecture about the unseen. The presence of the dog in this condition is part of God's care for them: just as He preserved them by turning them from the earth's destruction, He preserved them from enemies through a dog, so that they would be feared, along with the awe inherent in them. As He, Exalted, said: ﴿If you had looked upon them﴾, that is, had you gazed at them, despite the utmost of your strength in confronting battles, ﴿you would have turned from them in flight, and you would have been filled with dread of them﴾, that is, fear that fills your breast, because of the awe with which they were clothed. So no one's gaze falls upon them without him being awed and frightened of them. This, as Ibn Kathir said, is so that no one approaches them, and no hand touches them, until the Book reaches its term and their sleep, which God, blessed and exalted, willed for them, is complete, owing to the profound wisdom and vast mercy in that. And His saying, Exalted is He:

(p-4033) The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[19] ﴿And thus We roused them that they might question one another. A speaker among them said, "How long have you remained?" They said, "We have remained a day or part of a day." They said, "Your Lord knows best how long you have remained. So send one of you with this silver of yours to the city, and let him look for which of them has the purest food, and bring you provision from it; and let him be discreet, and let no one become aware of you."﴾

﴿And thus We roused them﴾ — that is: just as We put them to that sleep, We roused them with their bodies, hair and skin intact, not having lost anything of their forms or conditions, as a reminder of His power over causing sleep and resurrection alike. Ibn Kathir said: "And that was after three hundred and nine years."

His words, exalted is He, ﴿that they might question one another﴾ — that is: that some of them might ask others, and they might come to know their own condition and what God had done with them, so that they would take heed, draw evidence for the greatness of God's power, increase in certainty, and give thanks for what God had bestowed upon them and honoured them with. This is what az-Zamakhshari conveyed.

By this it becomes clear that the rousing is the cause of the questioning. As for one who makes the lam (in "that they might") denote consequence, he takes into account that the purpose of His action, exalted is He, is to manifest the perfection of His power. ﴿A speaker among them said, "How long have you remained?"﴾ — that is: how long did you sleep? (This is) an acknowledgement of his own ignorance, or a request for knowledge from others, even though it did not appear that he was certain. ﴿They said, "We have remained a day or part of a day."﴾ Ibn Kathir said: It seems that their entry into the cave was at the beginning of a day, and their waking was at the end of a day; for this reason they said, "or part of a day." Al-Mahayimi said: Whoever considers that they entered in the morning and woke in the evening thinks they remained a day; and whoever considers that some of the day remained thinks they remained part of a day. Thus, despite the marvels they were granted, they speak by conjecture. The friend of God may speak by conjecture regarding matters that are not among the fundamentals, and he may err. Az-Zamakhshari said: It is an answer based on the predominant assumption, and in it is evidence for the permissibility of ijtihad (independent reasoning, ijtihad) and of speaking on the basis of predominant assumption, and that it is not a lie, even if it may be an error.

﴿They said, "Your Lord knows best how long you have remained."﴾ — this is a rebuke to them from some of their own number, and that God knows best the duration of their stay. As if these people knew, through indications or through inspiration from God, that the period was long, and that its exact measure was unclear. So they left determining it to their Lord. ﴿So send one of you with this silver of yours﴾ — that is, the silver taken for provision. Al-Waraq is silver. ﴿to the city﴾ — that is, the one you fled from. ﴿Let him look for which of them has the purest food﴾ — that is, the best. ﴿and bring you provision from it; and let him be discreet﴾ — that is, in the transaction and in choosing the food; or in his conduct of concealment, so that he is not noticed regarding your condition and your religion. ﴿And let no one become aware of you.﴾

The commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 18, verse 20:

The discussion of His saying, exalted is He:

[20] ﴿Indeed, if they come to know of you, they will stone you or return you to their religion, and then you will never succeed, ever.﴾

﴿Indeed, if they come to know of you﴾ — they will discover your whereabouts. ﴿They will stone you﴾ — that is, they will kill you with stones. ﴿Or return you to their religion﴾ — that is, they will make you enter it by harsh compulsion. ﴿And then you will never succeed, ever﴾ — that is, if you return to their religion. Al-Qashani said: The dominance of the common people, the control of the blind followers (muqallidah) and the literalists (hashawiyyah) who are veiled, and of the people of falsehood who are sealed, their stoning of the people of truth, and their calling them to their religion, is evident, as it was in the early days of the Prophetic mission.

Subtleties:

The first: Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, how did they link their saying "so send one of you with this silver coin" to the discussion of the period of time? I say: it is as if they said, "Your Lord knows best about that; you have no way to know it, so turn to something else that concerns you." End of quote.

Al-Mahayimi held that their saying "so send" is part of the discussion of the period of time; they intended by it to investigate it. It is as if, when they referred the determination of it to God, the Exalted, with His saying, ﴿Your Lord knows best how long you have remained﴾ [al-Kahf: 19], they said: this referral does not prevent seeking knowledge of the period, even within another matter. So seek it within a need of ours, namely that one of you go with this silver of yours, so that we do not need to ask about the period, especially in a place that prevents answering the one asked about it, which leads to destruction.

The second: In (al-Iklil), it is said: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So send﴾ [al-Kahf: 19] and so on, is a basis for agency and representation. Ibn al-'Arabi said: it is the strongest verse in that regard.

Al-Kiya said: In it is evidence for the permissibility of mixing the dirhams of a group, buying with them, and eating food together among them as partners, even if they differ in how much they eat.

The third: His saying, exalted is He, concerning them, ﴿Then let him look which of them has the purest food﴾ [al-Kahf: 19], indicates the legitimacy of seeking out the best food and its finest quality to the greatest possible extent, by the form of the superlative (ahza, "purest"). For the purest nourishment, which meets the sanitary conditions, benefits the body, does not tire it, and does not harm it. Therefore, medically, care for its quality and purity is obligatory, as detailed in the laws of health.

The fourth: Al-Razi said: (al-Rajm) in the sense of killing is frequent in the revelation, as in His saying, ﴿Had it not been for your kinsmen, we would have stoned you﴾ [Hud: 91], and His saying, ﴿that you stone me﴾ [al-Dukhan: 20]. Its original meaning is throwing, that is, with stones (rijam), which are rocks. It is not far-fetched that the literal meaning is intended in all its occurrences, for added terror, since stoning is the most vile form of killing. And His saying, exalted is He:

**Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 18, verse 21:**

The discussion concerning the interpretation (ta'wil) of His saying, exalted is He:

[21] ﴿And thus We caused them to be found, that they might know that the promise of Allah is true and that the Hour, there is no doubt about it, when they disputed among themselves over their affair. So they said, "Build over them a structure; their Lord is most knowing of them." Those who prevailed in their affair said, "We will surely take over them a place of masjid (place of worship)."﴾

﴿And thus We caused them to be found﴾, i.e., just as We put them to sleep and raised them up for the wisdom in that, We made the people of the city aware of them, until the one they had sent for food entered it and brought out their old silver coins [p-4036] ﴿that they might know that the promise of Allah is true﴾, i.e., that those whom We made aware of their condition might know that Allah's promise of resurrection is true, because their state in their sleep and their waking after it was like the state of one who dies and then is resurrected. ﴿And that the Hour﴾, i.e., the one promised with the resurrection in it, ﴿there is no doubt about it﴾, since there must be recompense in accordance with wisdom.

Then He, exalted is He, pointed to what occurred concerning their affair after their death, and the concern of their people for guarding their graves, by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿when they disputed among themselves over their affair. So they said, "Build over them a structure"﴾, i.e., over the entrance of their cave, a great structure, like the khanqahs (lodges), the shrines, and the tombs built over the prophets and their followers. And "when" (idh), as it appears to me, is an adverb governed by an implied "remember" (udhkur). The sentence is a new beginning (mustaʾnifa) to explain the conclusion of their story with what happened after their death, following what had been summarized of their story after their resurrection and the discovery of them. To make it an adverb of ﴿We caused them to be found﴾, or of something else that they mentioned, has no strength of connection nor precision of meaning.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So they said﴾ is an explanation of what was disputed. His saying: ﴿their Lord is most knowing of them﴾ is a parenthetical sentence (jumla mu'tarida). It is either from Allah, as a refutation of those who delved into their discussion from among those disputants about them in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ) from the People of the Book, or it is from the words of the disputants in their time, as if they discussed their wondrous affair and debated their conditions and the length of their stay. When they could not find guidance, they referred the reality of their matter to Him, exalted is He. ﴿Those who prevailed in their affair﴾, i.e., among the disputants, who were the holders of dominance and the authority of the word, ﴿We will surely take over them a place of masjid﴾, i.e., we will pray in it, seeking blessing through them and their place.

**Note:**

Ibn Kathir said: Two opinions have been related about those who said this:

One of them: they were Muslims among them.

The second: they were polytheists.

The apparent meaning is that they were the people of influence. But is it praiseworthy or not? There is room for consideration in this, because the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "May Allah curse the Jews and the Christians, who took the graves of their prophets and righteous people as places of worship," warning against what they did. End of quote.

[p-4037] It is strange that he hesitated about whether they were not praiseworthy, while he cited after it the authentic hadith, recorded with the curse upon the one who does that, which is the gravest thing in which the wrath of Allah and His divine displeasure are expressed. The reason for this is that building over the grave of a prophet or a saint is a means of drawing attention to it and supplicating to it. Therefore it opens the door to shirk and is a means of approaching it by the nearest way. Is the origin of the worship of idols anything other than this? As Ibn Abbas said concerning the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And they said: "Do not leave your gods, nor leave Wadd, nor Suwa', nor Yaghuth, nor Ya'uq, nor Nasr"﴾ [Nuh: 23]. He said: These were righteous men among their people. When they died, they cleaved to their graves, then they made their images. When the period lengthened for them, they worshipped them. So these, when they intended to benefit from the dead, that led them to worship idols.

Imam Muhammad ibn Abd al-Hadi, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his book (al-Sarim al-Munakki), after citing what preceded: What clarifies this is that those among the people of shirk who spoke about visiting the dead explicitly stated that the aim is the benefit of the visitor from the one visited. They said: Part of the completeness of the visit is that he directs his resolve and his spirit toward the dead person and his grave. When the lights of the higher realms overflow upon the spirit of the dead, they overflow from it upon the spirit of the visitor through that attachment and direction toward the dead, just as light is reflected onto a transparent body by facing it.

This very meaning was mentioned by the worshippers of idols regarding visiting graves. It was received from them by those who received it without having comprehensive knowledge of shirk, its causes and its means. From here appears the secret of the intended aim of the Prophet (ﷺ) in his prohibition against glorifying graves, taking mosques over them, and lamps; his cursing of the one who does that and his informing about the severity of Allah's anger against him; his prohibition against praying toward them; his prohibition against taking his grave as a festival; and his supplication to his Lord, exalted is He, that He not make his grave an idol that is worshipped. This is his prohibition against glorifying graves. And that is his teaching and guidance for the visitor that he should intend the benefit of the dead, supplication for him, and kindness toward him, not supplication by him nor supplication at his grave.

[p-4038] Then he, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Whoever thinks that this is glorification of them is mistaken and ignorant. For their glorification is only by obeying them, following their command, loving them, and honoring them. So whoever glorifies them by that which disobeys them, that is not glorification at all, but rather its opposite, for it includes opposing them and disobeying them. If a servant prostrates to them, or calls upon them besides Allah, or glorifies them, or circumambulates their graves, and builds mosques and lamps over them, and attributes to them the characteristics of lordship, and exempts them from the requirements of servitude, and claims that this is glorifying them, he would be among the most ignorant and misguided of people. And this is of the same kind as the glorification of the Christians of the Messiah, to the point that they removed him from servitude. Whoever glorifies a created being with what that glorified one dislikes and hates, and whose doer he detests, has not in reality glorified him, but has treated him in the opposite manner of glorification. So the glorification of the Messenger (ﷺ) is that his commands be obeyed, his reports be believed, and nothing be placed before what he brought. Glorification is of two kinds: the first is what the one glorified loves, approves, commands, and praises its doer; this is glorification in reality. The second is what he dislikes, hates, and censures its doer; this is not glorification, but rather excess that contradicts glorification. For this reason, the Rafidah (Rafidites) were not glorifiers of Ali, by their claims of divinity, prophethood, infallibility, and the like. Nor were the Christians glorifiers of the Messiah by their claims about him, whatever they claimed. And the Prophet (ﷺ) denounced whoever glorified him with what he had not legislated. So he denounced Mu'adh for prostrating to him, and that is pure glorification.

In the Musnad (of Ahmad), with an authentic chain on the condition of Muslim, from Anas ibn Malik: "A man said: O Muhammad! O our master! Son of our master! O best of us! Son of the best of us! The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Keep to your piety, and let not Satan lead you astray. I am Muhammad ibn Abdullah, the servant of Allah and His Messenger. I do not like you to raise me above my station, which Allah, mighty and majestic, has placed me.'"

He (ﷺ) also said: "Do not exaggerate in praising me as the Christians exaggerated in praising Isa ibn Maryam. I am only a servant, so say: the servant of Allah and His Messenger." He used to dislike that his companions stand up for him when they saw him. He forbade them from praying behind him standing while he was ill, and he said: "If you were nearly to do the act of Persia and Rome, [p-4039] standing over their kings..." All of this is of the glorification that he dislikes and hates.

Some people have exaggerated in glorifying graves to the point that one of them said: Calamity is averted from the people of a town or region by means of the prophets and righteous ones buried among them. This is an excess that contradicts the religion of the Muslims, and contradicts the Book, the Sunnah, and the consensus (ijma'). There is an important continuation to this discussion; look into it.

**The discussion on the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:**

[22] ﴿They will say, "They were three, the fourth of them their dog." And they will say, "They were five, the sixth of them their dog," guessing at the unseen. And they will say, "They were seven, and the eighth of them their dog." Say, "My Lord knows best their number; none knows them except a few. So do not argue concerning them except with an outward argument, and do not seek a ruling about them from any of them."﴾

﴿They will say﴾, meaning: those who dispute about their story at the time of the Prophet ﷺ, from among the People of the Book, who have no real knowledge of the matter: ﴿"They were three, the fourth of them their dog." And they will say﴾, meaning: some others among them: ﴿"They were five, the sixth of them their dog, guessing at the unseen"﴾, meaning: throwing out and uttering words about what is hidden from them, that is, a conjecture devoid of certainty. Ibn Kathir said: "It is like one who shoots at a place he does not know; he hardly hits it, and if he does hit it, it is by chance." ﴿"And they will say, 'They were seven, and the eighth of them their dog.'"﴾ This is a report of the saying of another group who held this number. ﴿"Say, 'My Lord knows best their number; none knows them except a few.'"﴾, meaning: of those to whom God has granted knowledge of it. ﴿"So do not argue concerning them except with an outward argument"﴾, meaning: do not dispute with the People of the Book about the matter of the People of the Cave, except with a clear, gentle argument that does not delve deeply into it. This is in keeping with what the Noble Revelation has touched upon regarding their characterisation as guessing at the unseen and lacking knowledge, in a general manner, and with entrusting knowledge to God, glory be to Him, without ridiculing them or rebuking them when refuting them, as He said: ﴿"And argue with them in the best manner"﴾ [al-Nahl: 125], for knowledge of that matter does not entail any great benefit. It has been said: al-mira'ah (disputation) is al-mujadalah (argument). It has also been said that there is a distinction: al-mujadalah is contending in general, while al-mira'ah is contending in matters about which there is doubt (mirya), i.e. uncertainty, because it derives from (maraytu al-naqah), when you stroke the udder of the she-camel to draw milk. ﴿"And do not seek a ruling about them from any of them"﴾, meaning: do not ask any of them about their account, because asking is either for seeking guidance or for obstinacy and wrangling. They have no knowledge of that except what they say by guessing at the unseen, without relying on any infallible speech. Obstinacy in order to refute the opponent and to discredit what he has conflicts with noble morals. The meaning is: the truth that admits no doubt has come to you, and so it is the one that is put forward and judges over what preceded it of books and sayings.

**Remarks:**

**The first:** Most of the exegetes held that the last saying of the disputants, namely that they were seven and the eighth of them their dog, is the truth, because it was not described as guessing at the unseen as the first two were.

As for the specification of it by the particle waw in His words, ﴿"and the eighth of them"﴾, this is the waw that enters upon a clause functioning as a qualifier of an indefinite noun, to indicate the emphasis of the attachment of the qualifier to the qualified, and to show that his being characterised by it is a fixed and established matter, and that there is no number beyond it. As Ibn 'Abbas said: "When the waw came, the count ended." I say: The weakness of relying on these two aspects to strengthen the last saying is not hidden. For the absence of its characterisation as guessing at the unseen is only because what precedes it indicates this, and repeating it would impair the eloquence. The question of the waw is weaker than a spider's web. Such a dispute cannot be settled by a subtle and remote hint that borders on riddle, as is not hidden from one who has surveyed the instances of settling doubts in the Book, the Sunnah and the speech of the eloquent. Especially since the waw belongs to what is reported, not to the reporting, so it indicates its affirmation in the speaker's view, not in God's view, and thus it is not a hint at all. As for the answer of some that God, when He reported their saying before they uttered it, thus, He taught them to say it when they informed about Him with this expression, and that there is no barrier to its being part of the reporting, this is extremely far-fetched, an evident forcing, and a strange way of speaking.

Then it has been said: this clause is not necessarily a qualifier, since it may be a circumstantial clause (hal) of the indefinite noun, because its being joined by the waw is permissive. It may also be a predicate of an omitted subject, because it is permissible in such a case to include or omit the waw. Moreover, what they mentioned would only be complete if His words had not been followed by ﴿"Say, 'My Lord knows best their number.'"﴾ For in His ending of all the preceding sayings with this, there is a clear proof that they did not reach the correct number, and a guidance that the best course in such a situation is to refer knowledge to Him, exalted is He.

It also points to the fact that there is no need to delve into such matters without clear knowledge and a bright proof. And that if we are shown the decisive matter, we act upon it; otherwise, we abstain. This is confirmed by His words, glory be to Him, after it: ﴿"none knows them except a few"﴾, for in it is an indication that some of them are known to a group whom the Truth has not chosen to specify. These are either a prophet, or someone living in their time, or someone who investigated their story through sound report or received it from an infallible source. In it is also an announcement that He did not place a barrier over people's knowledge of the state of these men.

In sum, the noble text, with this style, does not indicate that the last saying is the truth, as you have come to know. As for what is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, his saying: "I am among the few whom God, mighty and majestic, excepted; they were seven," this is among the mawquf (reports ending with a Companion, not traced to the Prophet ﷺ). Had it been traced to the Prophet ﷺ and its chain been sound, we would act upon it, provided that it is recognised that Ibn 'Abbas differed in their number. For it is related from him that they were eight, as Ibn Ishaq related from Mujahid from him, and it is also related from him that they were seven, as related by Qatadah and Ikrimah from him. Then I saw that al-Razi quoted from al-Qadi that he said: "If Ibn 'Abbas knew it by the explanation of the Messenger, then it is sound; and if he relied on the particle waw, then it is weak." End of quotation. This is what has become clear to me now.

After I had written the above some time later, I came upon their account in (Tabaqat al-Shuhada al-Masihiyyin, the Classes of the Christian Martyrs) and that their number is seven according to them, as you will see at the end of the verses concerning them. It occurred to me that Ibn 'Abbas only affirmed what he affirmed, from what became strong for him from the indication of the verse, as those majority of exegetes mentioned, and from the widespread transmission of their number among their people and among those transmitted from them. Then the absence of objection to it confirmed and validated it. Likewise, Imam Taqi al-Din Ibn Taymiyyah, may God have mercy on him, affirmed the same, for he said in (a rule of his on exegesis): "This noble verse includes the etiquette in this situation, the situation of reporting sayings and teaching what is fitting in such a matter. For He, exalted, informed about them with three (p-4042) sayings, refuting the first two and remaining silent about the third, which indicates its soundness. For had it been false, He would have refuted it as He refuted the other two. Then He guided that acquiring knowledge of their number is of no benefit. Thus it is said regarding such matters: ﴿'Say, My Lord knows best their number'﴾, for none knows this except a few people to whom God has granted knowledge. Therefore He said: ﴿'So do not argue concerning them except with an outward argument'﴾, meaning: do not exert yourself in what has no benefit, and do not ask them about that, for they know of it nothing but guessing at the unseen. This is the best way of reporting disagreement: to comprehensively include the sayings on that matter, to draw attention to the sound among them, to nullify the false, and to mention the benefit and fruit of the disagreement, lest dispute and disagreement arise over what has no benefit, thereby occupying oneself with it instead of with what is more important. As for one who reports a disagreement on a question without comprehensively including the sayings of people on it, he is deficient, for the correct view may lie in what he omitted; or one who reports the disagreement and leaves it unqualified without drawing attention to the sound of the sayings, he is also deficient." End of his words, may God have mercy on him, and this is the decisive word in this matter.

**The second:** al-Razi said: "They have mentioned for the waw in His words ﴿'and the eighth of them'﴾ several aspects:

The first: what they mentioned, that it indicates that this saying is preferable to the rest of the sayings. You have already come to know what is wrong with it.

The second: that the number seven among the Arabs is the basis for hyperbole in counting. When they reach eight, they use a word that indicates resumption, so they say: "and eight." Thus this speech came according to this rule. They say: it is indicated by its parallel in three verses: His words ﴿"and those who forbid evil"﴾ [al-Tawbah: 112], for this is the eighth number of the preceding numbers; His words ﴿"until, when they reach it and its gates are opened"﴾ [al-Zumar: 73], because the gates of Paradise are eight and the gates of Hell are seven; and His words ﴿"previously married and virgins"﴾ [al-Tahrim: 5], because His words "and virgins" constitute the eighth of what precedes. People call this waw the waw of the eight, and its meaning is what we have mentioned."

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 18, verse 23–24:

The words of Allah the Exalted:

(p-4044) The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[23] ﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow,"﴾ [24] ﴿unless [you add], "If Allah wills." And remember your Lord when you forget and say, "I hope that my Lord will guide me to what is nearer than this to right guidance."﴾ [Al-Kahf: 24].

﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow,"﴾ ﴿unless [you add], "If Allah wills." And remember your Lord when you forget﴾ [Al-Kahf: 24]. In this verse there are several meanings. Among them: the meaning is "Do not say it except at the time Allah wills, by His permitting you to say it, so that you are speaking by His will." The will (mashi'ah) here therefore means permission (idhn), because the time of Allah's willing something is not known except by His permission regarding it, that is, His informing you of it. Among them: "Do not say, regarding an action you have resolved upon, 'Indeed, I will do that tomorrow,' except by saying with it, 'If Allah wills,' disavowing the necessity of dictating to Allah and of the action by your own will, but rather by the will of Allah, so that you act by His will." And so that there is no lie if Allah the Exalted did not will it. Among them: the meaning is "Do not say that while being decisive about doing it and definite about it, because: ﴿And no soul knows what it will earn tomorrow﴾ [Luqman: 34]. So it is not fitting to be certain and definite about an action in the unknown future."

And the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿unless [you add], "If Allah wills"﴾ [Al-Kahf: 24], that is: unless you say that definitive statement by forgetfulness; then, at that time, return to your Lord by remembering Him. For this reason He said: ﴿And remember your Lord when you forget﴾ [Al-Kahf: 24]. On all these aspects, "never say" (la taqulanna) is a prohibition coordinated with the two prohibitions before it. Al-Jahiz said in the Book of Animals (al-Hayawan): "Allah, majestic and exalted, only obliged His servant to say, 'If Allah wills,' in order to preserve a custom for the one who swears, and so that his speech and wording do not resemble the wording of one who is self-reliant and self-sufficient, and so that His servant remembers Allah, for he is a servant who is managed, turned about, made easy, and directed and subjected."

There remains another aspect: that the meaning is "Do not say that except if Allah wills that you say this statement." The sentence is declarative, intended to inform of the prior precedence of His will, exalted is He, over everything he resolves upon and says. Like His saying: (p-4045) ﴿And you will not will except that Allah wills﴾ [Al-Insan: 30]. This meaning is the apparent one at first glance, as he said in al-Intisaf. In the meaning there is an allusion that he, may Allah's blessings be upon him, had intended some matter concerning the news of these youths, and resolved upon a matter for the following day of the discussion about it.

Perhaps it was about consulting them about it. So when He forbade it, He informed that everything that exists is by His will, exalted is He, so that what he had said would enter into it at the first level. That is: what you said and resolved to do happened by the will of Allah, since Allah willed that you say it. The verse thus serves as care for him and gentleness in address, following what the prohibition alludes to of tenderness; and for this reason it intervened between the preceding prohibition on consulting them and the following command to remember Him when one forgets, that is, forgets what he was enjoined. By what we have mentioned, it is known that this meaning has a sound aspect.

As for the claim of al-Nasir in al-Intisaf that it is not the purpose, and that the purpose is the prohibition of this saying except when coupled with His will, exalted is He—this restricts the verse to one of its meanings, and goes to what is well known in its interpretation, and is a failure to reflect on this subtle meaning, and on the remaining other meanings that the noble wording admits. The strength of the last meaning has become clear due to its agreement with the verse: ﴿And you will not will except that Allah wills﴾ [Al-Insan: 30], and the Qur'an explains part of it by part. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

And the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And say, "I hope that my Lord will guide me to what is nearer than this to right guidance"﴾ [Al-Kahf: 24], that is, to good and benefit. The reference is to the news being discussed.

Notes:

The first: It is narrated that "he, may Allah's blessings be upon him, was asked about the People of the Cave, the Spirit, and Dhul-Qarnayn, and he said, 'I will answer you about them tomorrow,' and did not make an exception. So the revelation was withheld for fifteen days, then there was revealed: ﴿And never say...﴾ the verse." This narration has been discredited by al-Qadi—as related by al-Razi—on several grounds. And the truth is with him, because it is among the narrations of Ibn Ishaq, which contain an unknown (majhul) element, as Ibn Kathir and others transmitted it from him. And Allah knows best.

The second: The saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And say, "I hope that my Lord will guide me"﴾ [Al-Kahf: 24], and so on, points to the fact that this news is not something for which care should be taken in verifying it, refining its details, and seeking right guidance in it, to the extent of burdening oneself to give a fatwa to the People of the Book about it. The resolve to do something of what pertains to it in the future—since it is among the bygone matters, whose proper concern for the one who delves into them is to look at them from the aspect of the lesson and the benefits they contain, as the verses of the revelation have made firm regarding them.

The third: These etiquettes, I mean from His saying: ﴿So do not argue﴾ [Al-Kahf: 22] up to here, interrupted the account of their story before completing it, hastening to give attention to these etiquettes and to preserve them, so that they may take firmer hold and be rooted in the soul most firmly. And Allah knows best.

The fourth: It is narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And remember your Lord when you forget﴾ [Al-Kahf: 24]: if you forget to make the exception by the will (of Allah), then remember and make the exception; and that is (as al-Qurtubi said) to remedy the blessing and to be free from sin.

And al-Nasir said in al-Intisaf: As for the apparent meaning of the verse, it requires the command to make up for the exception whenever one remembers, even after a long time. As for its resolving the oath at that time, there is no evidence for it from it. End.

As for the claim that the apparent meaning is one of the aspects of it, based on the premise that the will in the verse before it is the will of speech, which is one of the meanings of the verse—it has been related from Ibn Abbas that making the exception is permissible even if much time has passed. Then there was disagreement from him: it was said up to a month, said up to a year, and said forever. In Husul al-Ma'mul: whoever says that this statement was not authentically from Ibn Abbas perhaps did not know that it is established in the Mustadrak of al-Hakim, where he said: "Sahih according to the conditions of the two Shaykhs," with the wording: "If a man swears an oath, he may make the exception up to a year." In sum, the narration from him, may Allah be pleased with him, is authentic, but the correct view is contrary to what he said.

Among them is the hadith of Abu Dawud and others: "By Allah! I will certainly raid Quraysh," then he was silent, then said: "If Allah wills." And among them is the hadith: "Its trees shall not be cut and its grass shall not be uprooted," whereupon al-Abbas said: "Except the idhkhir (grass)." This is in the Sahih. And among them is his saying, may Allah's blessings be upon him, at the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah: "Except Suhayl ibn Bayda." End. And the saying of Allah the Exalted:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 18, verse 25–26:

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[25] ﴿And they remained in their cave three hundred years and exceeded by nine.﴾ [26] ﴿Say, "Allah is most knowing of how long they remained. To Him belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth. How seeing of Him and hearing! They have not besides Him any protector, and He does not share His command with anyone."﴾ [al-Kahf: 26].

﴿And they remained in their cave three hundred years and exceeded by nine.﴾ ﴿Say, "Allah is most knowing of how long they remained."﴾ [al-Kahf: 26] This is a report of the saying of the People of the Book in his time (ﷺ), concerning the duration of their staying asleep in the cave to which they had resorted, so that they might devote themselves to the remembrance of Allah and His worship. He (exalted is He) refuted them with His words: ﴿Say, "Allah is most knowing of how long they remained."﴾ [al-Kahf: 26] This is the view taken by Qatadah and Mutarrif ibn 'Abd Allah. Qatadah supported it with the reading of Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him), "and they said, 'and they remained'." It has been said: according to this, the pronoun in ﴿and they exceeded﴾ refers to the People of the Book. In this, the reason for deviating from the apparent meaning, namely three hundred and nine years, becomes evident, even though it is shorter and clearer. This is because some of them (p-4048) said "three hundred," and others said "more by nine." The weakness of what has been mentioned is clear, for the pronoun refers to the youths. The reason for the deviation is to agree with the endings of the verses, which end with the accusative letter (nun). The claim of greater brevity is a grammatical nicety, which eloquence does not stand upon. As for greater clarity, sound taste rejects it, for the Arab sense finds between the two sentences a distance like that between the two easts in terms of pleasantness. The claim that in it there is an indication that it is three hundred by the reckoning of the People of the Book by days, taking the solar year, and three hundred and nine by the reckoning of the Arabs, taking the lunar year, as an explanation of the difference between them, since the difference between them is three years in every hundred years, is a claim whose soundness depends on establishing that the People of the Book reckoned by the solar year, and that He related to us what they intended by the lunar year. Therefore He said: "and they exceeded by nine," so that we may stop at determining what they meant. From where is that established? And what is the motive for this confused over-deepening? The verse is clear in itself regarding their claim of the duration of their stay. They may mean the solar or the lunar year, and whichever of them they said, He refuted them with His words: ﴿Say, "Allah is most knowing of how long they remained."﴾ [al-Kahf: 26], i.e., by the measure of their stay. So do not follow what you have no knowledge of, and what is unseen is referred back to Him, exalted is He, as He said: ﴿To Him belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth.﴾ [al-Kahf: 26], i.e., what is hidden and concealed in them of the conditions of their inhabitants; that is, He alone knows it. ﴿How seeing of Him and hearing!﴾ [al-Kahf: 26], i.e., how He sees each existent and hears each audible thing, nothing is hidden from Him, and nothing blocks His sight or His hearing.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He used a form that indicates wonder at His perception of things heard and seen, to show that His matter in perception is beyond the limit of what the hearers and seers perceive, because He perceives the subtlest and smallest things, just as He perceives the largest in bulk and densest in body, and He perceives the inner as He perceives the outer.

A subtle point:

In (al-Iklil) he said: al-Muntakhab used His words, exalted is He, ﴿How seeing of Him and hearing!﴾ [al-Kahf: 26] as evidence for permitting the use of the form of exclamation (ta'ajjub) in describing the attributes of Allah, exalted is He, like your saying: "How great is Allah and how majestic is He!" End.

That is, deriving the exclamatory form from the auditory attributes by analogy with what is in the verse, though it may be said that one should stop. It requires reflection.

As for His words, exalted is He: ﴿What they have﴾ [al-Kahf: 26], i.e., the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth in His creation: ﴿besides Him any protector﴾ [al-Kahf: 26], i.e., one who manages their affairs: ﴿and He does not share His command﴾ [al-Kahf: 26], i.e., His judgment: ﴿with anyone﴾ [al-Kahf: 26], i.e., of His created beings, above or below. Rather, He alone is singular in judgment and decree over them, and in their management and disposition, in whatever He wills and loves.

Al-Mahayimi said: In it there is an indication that their knowledge of them is either of the category of the unseen, in which case it is exclusive to Allah; or of the category of the audible, in which case He is the most hearing; or of the category of sight, in which case He is the most seeing. End. And it is very subtle. And His words, exalted is He:
