Al-Mahayimi said: In it there is an indication that their knowledge of them is either of the category of the unseen, in which case it is exclusive to Allah; or of the category of the audible, in which case He is the most hearing; or of the category of sight, in which case He is the most seeing. End. And it is very subtle. And His words, exalted is He:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[27] ﴿And recite what has been revealed to you of the Book of your Lord; none can alter His words, and you will not find any refuge other than Him.﴾

﴿And recite what has been revealed to you of the Book of your Lord⦆ means: by conveying what is in it. Among it is what has been revealed to you concerning the story of the youths, for it is the truth, about which no one needs to seek a ruling (istifta') beyond it.

Al-Qashani said: It is permissible for (min) [in "min kitab"] to denote the starting point (li-ibtida' al-ghayah). And "the Book" is the first Tablet (al-lawh al-awwal), comprising all the sciences, from which revelation was sent down to whoever was sent it. It is also permissible that it be an explanation of what was revealed.

﴿None can alter His words⦆ means: none can change them, distort them, or remove them.

Al-Qashani said: "His words" are the principles of monotheism (tawhid) and of enumeration (al-'add) and their types.

His aim is to repel what might arise from the occurrence of the abrogation (naskh) of some earlier laws by later ones and their replacement by them. So he indicated that abrogation applies only to the branches (al-furu'), not to the foundations (al-usul).

The more apparent meaning of the verse is that no one other than Him changes His ruling, as in His saying: ﴿There is no one to repel His judgment﴾ [al-Ra'd: 41]. As for Him, glory be to Him, He is the doer of what He wills.

﴿And you will not find any refuge other than Him⦆ means: no shelter (multaja').

(p-4050) Ibn Jarir took a course in interpreting this verse, saying: God, exalted is He, says to His Prophet: Follow what has been sent down to you of the Book of your Lord, and do not ever abandon its recitation and following what it contains of God's commands and prohibitions and acting upon its lawful and unlawful, lest you be among the ruined. That is because the destiny of whoever opposes it and abandons following it on the Day of Resurrection is Hell. ﴿None can alter His words⦆ means: none can change what He has threatened by His words which He sent down to you, against the people of His disobedience and those who act contrary to this Book which We revealed to you. His saying ﴿And you will not find any refuge other than Him⦆ means: and if you do not recite what has been revealed to you of the Book of your Lord, following it and taking it as your guide, then God's threat which He has promised against those who transgress His limits will befall you; you will not find, other than God, a refuge to turn to, nor an escape to turn away to from Him, because God's power encompasses you and all His creation, and none of them can flee from a matter He wills for them. End.

Note:

These youths, the People of the Cave, are mentioned in Christian histories, and an annual feast is held in their commemoration on the twenty-seventh day of the month of Tammuz, because they were persecuted by the Greek rulers for their belief in God alone, their entry into the Christian religion, and their rejection of the idolatry that the Greeks practised. I have seen in the book (al-Kanz al-Thamin fi Akhbar al-Qiddisin) an extensive account of their circumstances under the heading (Concerning the Seven Holy Martyrs of Ephesus), from which we excerpt what follows, to refute the claim of one who fabricates that their story is not known at all, as I read in some books of the unbelievers.

The author of the account said: These seven martyrs were brothers by blood. Their names: Maximianus, Malchus, Martinianus, Dionysius, John, Serapion, then Constantine. These young men offered their lives as a sacrifice for Christ, near the city of Ephesus, around the year (252) of the Christian era, in the time of the harsh persecution which King Decius waged against the Christians.

The Christians honoured them as true martyrs. Panegyrics are delivered for them in the churches, in which their virtuous qualities are proclaimed on the day of their martyrdom there, on the fourth day of the month of Ab, which is devoted to commemorating the miracle through which their holy bodies appeared in the western cave of the city of Ephesus.

He then said: As for the manner of their martyrdom, it is not known, for their struggles in the path of faith were not recorded in the careful ecclesiastical histories. Rather, what is affirmed about them is that their martyrdom took place in the time of King Decius, near the city of Ephesus, where their bodies were later found in a cave not far from the people of this city.

He then said: Some of the church writers hold that when these youths hid themselves in that cave to flee the persecution, their affair became known, and the entrance of the cave was closed upon them with great rocks, and thus they died within it. Others narrate that they were killed for the sake of faith in the city of Ephesus, and after their death their bodies were moved and buried in the said cave. Still others suppose that they imprisoned themselves alive by hiding in the said cave, so as to die by their own consent, fleeing the danger of the kinds of cruel torment which the Christians were undergoing in that savage persecution.

He then said: Whatever the manner of the martyrdom of these seven, it is established that God willed to honour them by manifesting their bodies through a heavenly vision. That was on the 4th of Ab, in the year 447, in the reign of the king (Theodosius the Younger).

He then said: It has become current on the lips of the peoples that these youths, after the entrance of the cave was closed upon them by the order of King Decius, did not die within it, neither a natural death nor a forced one, but slept a sleep for a period of about two hundred years. Then they rose from their natural sleep in the year (447).

He then said: Some historians have gone to interpret what is narrated of their long sleep, that when their bodies appeared intact from decay, after they had been buried in that cave alive or dead, by some extraordinary means, (p-4052) and were moved from their place of burial in which they had been, those bodies were regarded as if they had been found awakened from a sweet sleep in which they had been lying. However, what refutes this interpretation is what was narrated afterward from the Synaxarium, that they rose after having slept several years and triumphed over the error of those idolaters; and by their appearance in that state they confirmed the truth of their faith and strengthened the believers in the hope of the Resurrection to eternal life.

This is what we have excerpted from the book (al-Kanz al-Thamin), and by it you know what the People of the Book, the Christians, hold of disagreement among themselves, which the Noble Qur'an has pointed to. In the (Church History) it has come: The sayings and deeds of the martyrs in Christianity have only a little preserved, because most of them were burned by fire for a period of ten years, from the year (293) to (303). And from the eighth century onward, the Romans and Latins took care to gather the lives of the early martyrs. However, the most discerning, even those within the bosom of the Roman Church, now concede that most of the reports are fabricated narratives, out of love for eloquence. And the catalogues of saints called (Sayings of the Martyrs) are no more trustworthy, which were composed by ignorant people who were not capable, or into which falsehoods have entered since then. Thus this section of the Church's history of that time is dark, devoid of light. End of his words verbatim.

In it there is an inclination toward fairness regarding the lack of trust in what they possess of this disagreement, which the Noble Qur'an has settled at its root and uprooted from its foundations.

The Hafiz Ibn Kathir said, in commenting on His saying, exalted is He: "And when We said to the angels," the verse that follows, excusing what he had narrated, the gist of which is: Many narrations have been reported on this from the early generations, most of them from the Israelite narratives, which are related so that one may examine them. God knows best the state of many of them. Some of them may be definitively judged false because they contradict the truth in our hands. The Qur'an is sufficient without all other earlier reports, for they are scarcely free of alteration, addition, and omission. Many things have been fabricated in them. They do not have among their memorizers the precise guardians who can clear them of the distortion of the exaggerators and the forgery of the falsifiers, as this Ummah has among its imams and scholars, its masters and the pious, its eminent critics, and its memorizers who recorded the Hadith and edited it, and distinguished its sound from its good, its disapproved, its fabricated, and its abandoned, and who knew the forgers, the liars, and the unknown among the categories of narrators. All of this is to safeguard the Prophetic threshold and the Muhammadan station, seal of the messengers and master of mankind, from being attributed to him a lie or narrated from him what is not from him. May God be pleased with them and make them content, and make the Gardens of Paradise their abode. And so He has done. And His saying, exalted is He:

The discourse on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[28] ﴿And restrain yourself to be with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His Face. And let not your eyes pass beyond them, desiring the adornment of the worldly life. And do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance, who follows his desire and whose affair has been [ever] in neglect.﴾

﴿And restrain yourself﴾, i.e., hold it back and make it firm; ﴿to be with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening﴾, i.e., with your companions who remember Him, glorified is He, at the two ends of the day, by consistently performing the prayer at both times; ﴿seeking His Face﴾, i.e., His Essence, seeking His good pleasure and obedience, not some passing good of the worldly life; ﴿And let not your eyes pass beyond them﴾, i.e., do not let your gaze go past them to others by turning away from them; ﴿desiring the adornment of the worldly life﴾, i.e., seeking the company of the nobles and the wealthy in order to win their hearts. ﴿And do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance﴾, i.e., We made it heedless, since its readiness for remembrance has utterly been nullified; or We found it heedless of Remembrance. This is so that it does not lead you to heedlessness of Him. ﴿who follows his desire and whose affair has been [ever] in neglect﴾, i.e., abandoned, treated with contempt, and wasted; or [it means] regret or excess. In the expression referring to the one commanded to be patient with them and the one forbidden to obey them, the relative pronoun is used to indicate the causal link of what is contained in the relative clause.

Ibn Jarir said: "A group of the chiefs of the polytheists saw the Prophet ﷺ sitting with Khabbab, Suhayb and Bilal. So they asked him to remove them from him when they came. And in a narration from Ibn Zayd: they said to him, may the blessings of Allah be upon him: 'We are ashamed to sit with so-and-so, and so-and-so, and so-and-so, so keep them away and sit with the nobles of the Arabs,' and the verse was revealed: ﴿And restrain yourself﴾."

Muslim narrated from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who said: "We were with the Prophet ﷺ, six men. The polytheists said to the Prophet ﷺ: 'Drive these away, so that they do not dare against us.' He said: I was there, and Ibn Mas'ud, and a man from Hudhayl, and Bilal, and two men whose names I have forgotten. So what Allah willed to occur occurred in the soul of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he spoke to himself. So Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed: ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord﴾ [al-An'am: 52], the verse."

Ibn Kathir said: Muslim alone narrated it, not al-Bukhari. And His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 18, verse 29:

The discussion of His saying, exalted is He:

[29] ﴿And say, "The truth is from your Lord, so whoever wills - let him believe; and whoever wills - let him disbelieve. Indeed, We have prepared for the wrongdoers a Fire whose walls will surround them. And if they ask for relief, they will be relieved with water like murky oil, which scalds the faces. Wretched is the drink, and evil is the resting place."﴾

﴿And say, "The truth is from your Lord"﴾ meaning: it has come with the truth, which is what has been revealed to me from Him, exalted is He. ﴿So whoever wills - let him believe; and whoever wills - let him disbelieve﴾: this may be part of what he is commanded to say, and the "fa" (فَ, "so") indicates the consequence of what follows upon what precedes, in the manner of a threat. That is: following the establishment that what has been revealed to me is the truth, without doubt, and that this truth is from your Lord. Whoever wills to believe in it, let him believe like the rest of the believers, and let him not make excuses with what hardly serves as an excuse. And whoever wills to disbelieve in it, let him do so. In this is, by way of threat and of displaying independence from following them, and indifference to them and to their faith, both in its existence and its absence, what is not hidden. Or it is a threat from God, exalted is He, (p-4055) and the "fa" indicates that what follows is a threat upon the command. The meaning: say to them that. And after that, whoever wills to believe in it, or to believe you in it, let him believe; and whoever wills to disbelieve in it, or to deny you in it, let him do so. This is what Abu al-Su'ud conveyed. In (al-Inaya): the command and the giving of choice are not on their literal reality; rather, it is a metaphor for indifference and disregard of it. The command to disbelieve is not intended; it is a metaphor for abandonment and leaving alone, by likening the state of one who is such to the state of one commanded to oppose. The aspect of similarity is indifference and disregard in both. This is like his saying: "Treat us harshly or treat us well, there is no blame upon us." This is a rebuttal of them in their call to drive away the poor believers so that he would sit with them and they would follow him. It was said to them: your faith's benefit returns only to you, so we do not care about it so that we would drive them away for that, after the truth has become clear and manifest. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We have prepared for the wrongdoers a Fire﴾ is a severe warning, a confirmation of the threat, and a justification for what it implies of deterrence from disbelief, or for what is understood from the apparent sense of the giving of choice, of indifference to their disbelief and little concern in deterring them from it. For preparing its recompense is among the motives for leniency and respite. And according to the first aspect, it is a justification for the command with what has been mentioned of the threatening choice. That is: say to them that: ﴿Indeed, We have prepared for the wrongdoers﴾, meaning: We have readied for the disbelievers in the truth, after it has come from God, glory be to Him. Expressing them by "the wrongdoers" is to alert that willing disbelief and choosing it is a transgression of the limit and placing a thing in other than its place. This is what Abu al-Su'ud conveyed. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Its walls will surround them﴾, meaning: its tent. Suradiq is the tent. It is used as a likeness for what encompasses them of the Fire, for the spreading of the flame of the Fire in all directions resembles the suradiq. And suradiq is also applied to the enclosure around the tent to prevent access to it. It likens what encompasses them of Hell to it. One says: a house that is surdaq, possessing a suradiq. ﴿And if they ask for relief﴾, meaning: from thirst, because their hearts are burnt, ﴿they will be relieved with water like murky oil﴾, meaning: like molten metal and like the dregs of oil. Al-Qashani said: of the kind of ghassaq and ghislin, that is: foul, putrid waters that flow from the bodies of the people of the Fire, blackened, with which they are given relief; or their filthy washings. This is supported by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and he is given to drink of water of pus﴾ [Ibrahim: 16], ﴿which he gulps down﴾ [Ibrahim: 17]. ﴿It scalds the faces﴾, meaning: when it is brought to him to drink, due to the extreme intensity of its heat.

(p-4056) ﴿And evil is it as a resting place﴾, meaning: the Fire is evil as a reclining place (mutaka'). The original meaning of irtifaq is placing the elbow beneath the cheek. Its mention is for the sake of parallelism with His saying: ﴿and good as a resting place﴾ [al-Kahf: 31]; otherwise, there is no reclining or leaning for the people of the Fire. It may also be sarcasm, as in the saying of the poet:

"I could not sleep, so I spent the night reclining (murtafiqan), as if in my eyes is bitter aloes, slaughtered."

Al-sabb is a bitter tree whose water burns the eye. Madhbuh means split. In the book Tanzil al-Ayat, in al-Sihah: "So-and-so spent the night murtafiqan," meaning reclining on the elbow of his hand. This is the posture of the grieving and the regretful. Thus, according to this, it is neither parallelism nor sarcasm, but its literal meaning. Just as it is for comfort, it is also for grief. (al-Inaya) followed up on this, saying: As for placing the hand beneath the cheek for grief and regret, the apparent meaning is that the punishment preoccupies them from it, so it is not possible for them, unless this is literal and not parallelism; therefore they did not turn to it. Then he gave the reason for urging faith, which is understood from the preceding giving of choice, with His saying, glory be to Him:

**The interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:**

[30] ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, indeed We do not allow the reward of one who does good deeds to be lost.﴾ [31] ﴿For them are gardens of perpetual residence, beneath which rivers flow. They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold, and they will wear green garments of fine silk and brocade, reclining therein upon couches. Excellent is the reward, and good is the resting place.﴾ [Al-Kahf: 31].

﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, indeed We do not allow the reward of one who does good deeds to be lost.﴾ ﴿For them are gardens of perpetual residence, beneath which rivers flow. They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold, and they will wear (p-4057) green garments of fine silk﴾ [Al-Kahf: 31]. "Sundus" is that which is thin of brocade (dibaj). ﴿And brocade﴾ [Al-Kahf: 31], which is that which is thick of it. ﴿Reclining therein upon couches﴾ [Al-Kahf: 31], i.e., thrones, in the manner of those who live in luxury. ﴿Excellent is the reward﴾ [Al-Kahf: 31], i.e., the aforementioned gardens. ﴿And good is the resting place﴾ [Al-Kahf: 31], i.e., a place of reclining. It was said that "murtafaq" means the dwelling and the abode, based on the verse: ﴿Indeed, it is evil as a settlement and residence﴾ [Al-Furqan: 66], and the verse ﴿Good as a settlement and residence﴾ [Al-Furqan: 76].

**The interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:**

[30] ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, indeed We do not allow the reward of one who does good deeds to be lost.﴾ [31] ﴿For them are gardens of perpetual residence, beneath which rivers flow. They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold, and they will wear green garments of fine silk and brocade, reclining therein upon couches. Excellent is the reward, and good is the resting place.﴾ [Al-Kahf: 31].

﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, indeed We do not allow the reward of one who does good deeds to be lost.﴾ ﴿For them are gardens of perpetual residence, beneath which rivers flow. They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold, and they will wear (p-4057) green garments of fine silk﴾ [Al-Kahf: 31]. "Sundus" is that which is thin of brocade (dibaj). ﴿And brocade﴾ [Al-Kahf: 31], which is that which is thick of it. ﴿Reclining therein upon couches﴾ [Al-Kahf: 31], i.e., thrones, in the manner of those who live in luxury. ﴿Excellent is the reward﴾ [Al-Kahf: 31], i.e., the aforementioned gardens. ﴿And good is the resting place﴾ [Al-Kahf: 31], i.e., a place of reclining. It was said that "murtafaq" means the dwelling and the abode, based on the verse: ﴿Indeed, it is evil as a settlement and residence﴾ [Al-Furqan: 66], and the verse ﴿Good as a settlement and residence﴾ [Al-Furqan: 76].

The discussion concerning the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[32] ﴿And present to them the parable of two men: We had granted one of them two gardens of grapevines, and We had surrounded them with date palms, and We had placed between them cultivated land.﴾

﴿And present to them a parable﴾, i.e., for the believer and the disbeliever: ﴿two men, to one of whom We had granted two gardens of grapevines, and We had surrounded them with date palms﴾, and these are the most precious things those people prefer, namely the enclosing of their vineyards with trees. ﴿And We had placed between them﴾, i.e., between the two gardens, or between the palms and the grapevines: ﴿cultivated land﴾, i.e., from them came fruits and staple foods, and so they were the source of wealth and status.

The discussion of the words of His, the Exalted:

[33] ﴿Both gardens yielded their produce and did not fall short therein of anything, and We caused a river to gush forth within them.﴾

﴿Both gardens yielded their produce﴾ — i.e., their fruit, in full. ﴿And did not fall short therein of anything﴾ — i.e., did not diminish. ﴿And We caused a river to gush forth within them﴾ — i.e., between them. ﴿A river﴾ — i.e., one that irrigates the trees and crops, and adds to the delight of their sight, completing their beauty.

The discussion of the words of His exalted saying:

[34] ﴿And he had fruit, so he said to his companion while he was disputing with him, "I am greater than you in wealth and mightier in men."﴾

﴿And he had﴾ i.e., the owner of the two gardens: ﴿fruit﴾ i.e., kinds of wealth other than the two gardens. From (p-4058) "thammara mālahu" (he multiplied his wealth), meaning he increased it. ﴿So he said to his companion while he was disputing with him﴾ i.e., replying to him in speech, reproaching him for his poverty and boasting over him with his wealth and standing: ﴿"I am greater than you in wealth and mightier in men"﴾ i.e., in supporters and retinue.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 18, verse 35:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[35] ﴿And he entered his garden while he was wronging himself. He said, "I do not think that this will ever perish."﴾

﴿And he entered his garden﴾ That is, with his companion, walking him around in it and boasting to him about it, as the context and his dialogue with him indicate. The singular "garden" here, although he had two gardens as mentioned earlier, is either because the purpose does not concern their multiplicity, or because one of them is joined to the other, or because entering happens one garden at a time. It has been said: the idafah (annexation construction) comes to convey the meaning of the lam (of possession), so what is meant by it is generality and comprehensiveness, that is, every garden that belongs to him, he enjoys it. Thus it conveys what the dual conveys, with an addition, which is the indication that he has no garden other than this one.

﴿while he was wronging himself﴾ That is, by doing what necessitates the removal of the blessing, namely disbelief and self-admiration. In al-'Inayah it is said that his wronging of it (the garden) is either in the sense of diminishing it and harming it, by exposing its blessing to decline and himself to ruin, or in the sense of placing a thing in other than its proper place, because what befits what he witnessed is humble weeping, not self-admiration with it and his thinking that it will never perish. The disbelief lies in denying the Resurrection, as His saying indicates: ﴿He said, "I do not think that this will perish"﴾, that is, be destroyed and pass away, ﴿this﴾, that is, the garden, ﴿ever﴾, due to his belief in the eternity of time and that there is no existence other than what his senses perceive. Therefore he said:

The Discourse on the Interpretation of His Words, exalted is He:

[36] ﴿And I do not think the Hour will ever come. And if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely find better than this as a return.﴾

﴿And I do not think the Hour will ever come﴾ i.e., will occur. His saying ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely find better than this as a return﴾ is an oath from him that, if he is returned to his Lord, on the basis of supposition and assumption, as his companion claims, he will surely find in the Hereafter something better than his garden in this world, out of presumption and wishful thinking regarding Allah, and a claim to His honor toward him and his station with Him. And indeed, He gave him the two gardens only because of his supposed deservingness and merit, and that this deservingness is with him wherever he turns. Like His saying: ﴿Indeed, with Him is the best [reward] for me﴾ [Fussilat: 50] and ﴿I will surely be given wealth and children﴾ [Maryam: 77]. And ﴿a return﴾ means a place of return and an outcome. This is what al-Zamakhshari conveyed.

Al-Mahayimi said: He disbelieved by saying the world is eternal, denying the resurrection of bodies, and believing in the reversal of recompense, when he said ﴿I will surely find better than this as a return﴾. The claim that the world is eternal negates the choice and will of the Creator. And denying the resurrection of bodies negates His power to restore them. And reversing recompense negates Divine wisdom.

Then Allah the Exalted related what his companion, the believer, replied to him, admonishing him and rebuking him for the disbelief in Allah and the self-deception he was in, by saying:

The discussion of the interpretation (ta'wil) of His, the Exalted's, words:

[37] ﴿His companion said to him, while he was conversing with him: "Do you disbelieve in the One who created you from dust, then from a drop of semen, then fashioned you into a man?"﴾

﴿His companion said to him﴾, meaning the one who reproached him for his poverty, rebuking him for his disbelief. ﴿And he was conversing with him﴾, meaning he was responding to him, returning his words of reproach for his disbelief, as the other had been reproaching him for his poverty, within the context of denouncing him: ﴿Do you disbelieve in the One who created you from dust, then from a drop of semen?﴾, meaning: He who made the dust into plants, then made them into food from which the semen is generated. ﴿Then fashioned you into a man﴾, meaning: He balanced you and perfected you as a human being, a male who reached the stage of adult men.

Abu al-Su'ud said: The expression of Him, the Exalted, by the relative pronoun (al-mawsul, "the One who") serves to indicate that what follows it in the relative clause is the cause, in order to denounce disbelief, and to allude to the proof of resurrection, which His words, the Mighty and Majestic, express: ﴿O mankind, if you are in doubt about the resurrection, then indeed We created you from dust﴾ [al-Hajj: 5]. And as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿How can you disbelieve in Allah, when you were dead and He gave you life?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 28].

Ibn Kathir said: That is, how can you deny your Lord, when His proof against you is manifest and clear, and everyone knows it from his own self. For there is no created being that does not know that it was non-existent and then came into existence, and its existence was not from itself, nor was it dependent on anything (p-4060) among the created beings, since it is like them. Thus he knows that its bringing into existence is ascribed to its Creator, who is Allah, there is no god but He, the Creator of everything. Hence his companion, the believer, said:

On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[38] ﴿But as for me, He is Allah, my Lord, and I ascribe no partner to my Lord, anyone.﴾

﴿But as for me, He is Allah, my Lord, and I ascribe no partner to my Lord, anyone.﴾ That is: "But as for me, I do not speak with your statement; rather, I acknowledge to Allah His oneness (wahdaniyyah) and His lordship (rububiyyah). And I ascribe no partner to Him, anyone along with Him, of the higher beings or the lower beings." Ibn 'Amir recited ﴿لَكِنّا﴾ (lakinna, "but I") with the alif affirmed both in connection and in pause. The rest read it without the alif in connection, and with it in pause, so the pausal reading is agreed upon. Its origin is "lakinna ana" (لَكِنَّ أنا). It was also recited in that form, so the hamzah was dropped, then the nun was assimilated into the like letter, becoming "lakinna" (لَكِنَّ), and then the alif was added, treating the connected form as the pausal form. This is because pausing on "ana" is with the alif, and because the alif indicates that the original is "lakinna ana," whereas without it there would be confusion between it and the emphatic "lakinna" (لَكِنَّ, "but").

Al-Zamakhshari said: Similar to it is the saying of the poet:

"And you shoot me with a glance" — that is, "you are the guilty one" — "and you make me hate you, but as for you, I do not hate you"

That is, "but as for I, I do not hate you." Close to it is the saying of another:

"Had you been a Dabbi, you would have known my kinship, but [you are] a Zanji with large lips"

That is, "but you [are]."

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 18, verses 39–41:

His saying, may He be exalted:

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, may He be exalted:

[39] ﴿And why, when you entered your garden, did you not say, "What Allah wills [will be]; there is no power except in Allah"? If you see me as less than you in wealth and children,﴾ [40] ﴿perhaps my Lord will give me something better than your garden and send upon it a calamity from the sky, so that it becomes barren land, slippery,﴾ [Al-Kahf: 40] [41] ﴿or its water will sink away, and you will never be able to find it.﴾ [Al-Kahf: 41].

﴿And why, when you entered your garden, did you not say, "What Allah wills"﴾ That is: why did you not say that when entering it? Al-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible for "ma" to be a relative pronoun in the nominative position, as the predicate of an elided subject, its estimated form being "the matter is what Allah wills"; or it may be a conditional in the accusative position, with the apodosis elided, meaning "whatever Allah wills, it comes to be." Its parallel in eliding the answer with "law" is in His saying: ﴿And if there were a Qur'an by which mountains could be moved﴾ [Al-Ra'd: 31]. The meaning is: why did you not say, upon entering it and looking at what Allah has provided you from it, "The matter is what Allah wills," acknowledging that it and every good in it came about only by the will and bounty of Allah, and that its affair is in His hand: if He wills, He leaves it flourishing, and if He wills, He ruins it. And [why did you not say], "There is no power except in Allah," affirming that whatever strength you relied upon for its cultivation and the management of its affairs is only by His aid and support, since no one is strong in his body or in the possession of his hand except by Allah, exalted is He. The purpose of the two sentences is disavowal of power and strength, and attributing what one has been given to the will of Allah and His power alone. Then his companion pointed out to him that his reproach of him for poverty may well be reversed, by his saying: ﴿If you see me as less than you in wealth and children,﴾ ﴿perhaps my Lord will give me﴾ [Al-Kahf: 40], that is, in this world as well: ﴿something better than your garden and send upon it a calamity﴾ [Al-Kahf: 40], that is, a measure decreed and reckoned by Allah, namely the judgment of its destruction by thunderbolts and heavenly afflictions: ﴿from the sky, so that it becomes barren land, slippery﴾ [Al-Kahf: 40], that is, smooth dust in which no foot can stand, because of its smoothness, (p-4062) or He destroys it by a calamity from below the earth, such that ﴿its water sinks away﴾ [Al-Kahf: 41], that is, sinks into the earth, ﴿and you will never be able to find it﴾, that is, a means by which to reach it, by digging or otherwise.

Note:

Each of His saying, ﴿If you see me﴾ and His saying, ﴿that He give me﴾ [Al-Kahf: 40], is written without a yā' (ya), because they are among the additional yā's (yā' al-zawā'id). As for pronunciation, some of the Seven Readers affirm it and some of them omit it.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 18, verse 42:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[42] ﴿And his fruit was encompassed (by ruin), so he began to wring his hands over what he had spent upon it, while it lay collapsed on its trellises, and he said, "Would that I had not associated anyone with my Lord."﴾

﴿And his fruit was encompassed﴾ means: by its destruction, so that He left him no fruit in it. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Uhita bihi (was encompassed) is an expression for its destruction. Its origin is from (when the enemy encompassed them, man ahata bihi al-'aduww), because when someone is encompassed, he has been taken possession of and overpowered. Then it came to be used for every destruction, and from it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿unless you are encompassed (by it)﴾ [Yusuf: 66]."

Similar to it is their saying, "Ata 'alayhi" (it came upon him), meaning he destroyed it, from "ata 'alayhimu al-'aduww" (the enemy came upon them) when he came to them overpowering them. This means that it is a figurative metaphor (isti'arah tamthiliyyah). He likened the destruction of his two gardens and what was in them to the destruction of a people by an enemy army that encompassed them and fell upon them such that none of them escaped. Just as ("ata 'alayhim") in the sense of "ahlakahum" (destroyed them) is also a metaphor, from the coming of a dominant enemy who prevails over them by force.

﴿So he began to wring his hands over what he had spent upon it﴾ means: he regretted his own state far more than his companion's rebuke of him and his companion's rebuke of him. Al-Zamakhshari said: "The turning of the two palms is a metaphor (kinayah) for regret and grief, because the one who regrets turns his palms from back to front, just as biting the hand and falling into the hand (al-suqut fi al-yad) are used as metaphors for that. And because it carries the meaning of regret, it takes the complement with (ʿalā) as if it were said: 'so he began to regret what he had spent upon it,' i.e., on its cultivation. So it is an adverbial phrase of redundancy (zarf laghw). It may also be a stable adverbial phrase (zarf mustaqarr) whose complement is specific, and it is a circumstantial state (hal), i.e., grieving. And tahassur is sorrow, which is more specific than regret, because it is (as al-Raghib said) grief over what has escaped."

﴿while it lay collapsed on its trellises﴾ means: fallen upon them. And ("al-'urush") is the plural of ("'arsh"), which is what is constructed so that a thing may be placed upon it. When it falls, what is upon it falls. This means that its trellised vines had their supports collapse onto the ground, and the vines fell on top of them, such that they came close to becoming bare, slippery earth.

﴿and he said﴾ is conjoined to ("yuqallibu"): ﴿"Would that I had not associated anyone with my Lord"﴾ means: from among the idols. That is because he remembered his brother's admonition and so knew that he had been brought to ruin through his polytheism and transgression. So he wished that he had not been a polytheist, so that God would not have destroyed his garden.

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

[43] ﴿And he had no company (fi'ah) to help him against Allah, nor was he able to defend himself.﴾

﴿And he had no company (fi'ah)﴾ meaning: a protection, and a group. ﴿To help him against Allah﴾ meaning: who would be able to aid him against Allah, just as he had boasted of them and grown proud over his companion. ﴿Nor was he able to defend himself﴾ meaning: he could not protect himself, by his own self and strength, from the retribution of Allah.

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, Exalted is He:

[44] ﴿There, guardianship belongs to God, the True. He is best in reward and best in outcome.﴾

﴿There, guardianship belongs to God, the True﴾ means: in that station and that state in which the destruction took place. (Al-walāya) with a fatḥa on the waw means victory (al-nuṣra), belonging to God alone; no one besides Him is able to grant it. The sentence thus confirms and emphasizes His words, ﴿and he had no company to help him﴾ [al-Kahf: 43], since it has the same meaning. Or it means that He grants victory therein to His believing friends over the polytheists, avenges them, and heals their hearts from their enemies, just as He gave victory over the disbeliever to his companion, the believer. And the words of the latter were fulfilled: ﴿It may be that my Lord will give me something better than your garden and send upon it a torment from the heaven﴾ [al-Kahf: 40]. It is reinforced by His words, ﴿He is best in reward and best in outcome﴾, meaning for His friends. Thus no believer's rank is diminished in this world, and no disbeliever's punishment is left aside out of regard for his nobility; rather, He punishes him for his sin and shows the believer's superiority over him.

It has also been read as (al-wilāya) with a kasra on the waw, meaning sovereignty and dominion. That is: there, (p-4064) sovereignty and dominion belong to Him; none overcomes Him or escapes Him. Or, in such a severe situation, every person in distress turns to God and believes in Him. The meaning is that he said, "Would that I had not associated anyone with my Lord," a word he was compelled to utter out of dismay at the calamity that befell him from the evil of his disbelief; had it not been for that, he would not have said it. This is like His words: ﴿And when they saw Our might, they said, "We believe in God alone and disbelieve in what we used to associate with Him."﴾ [Ghafir: 84]

And like His words, relating of Pharaoh: ﴿Until, when drowning overtook him, he said, "I believe that there is no god except the one in whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am among the Muslims."﴾ [Yunus: 90] ﴿Now? And you had disobeyed before and were among the corrupters.﴾ [Yunus: 91]

Or (there) indicates the Hereafter, meaning: in that abode guardianship belongs to God. This is like His words: ﴿Whose is the dominion today?﴾ [Ghafir: 16], and it fits His words, ﴿He is best in reward and best in outcome.﴾ As for (there), on the aforementioned readings, it is a predicate preceding (the guardianship), which is a postponed subject. The pause is at (victorious). Some have permitted (there) to be an object governed by (victorious), with the pause on it, and the phrase (the guardianship belongs to God) being a separate nominal sentence. That is: and he was not victorious in that land where the punishment of God descended; so there was no one to rescue him from it.

I say: this last view is extremely weak, and it breaks the rhyme-endings of the verses of the sūrah, for all of them are terminated with the accusative noun. Its proponent's basis is that it is grammatically permissible. But not everything grammatically permissible is refined in its eloquence. For this reason al-Zamakhsharī and those who followed him did not rely upon it. (al-Ḥaqq) is read in the nominative as an adjective of (al-walāya), in the accusative as a verbal object emphasizing the content of the sentence, governed by a implied verb, and in the genitive as an adjective of the divine name (Allāh). (ʿUqban) is read with a sukūn on the qāf and with a ḍammah on it; both mean the outcome, like al-ʿushur and al-ʿushr.

Note:

Many exegetes mention here an opinion regarding this parable: that the two men mentioned in it existed and had a known story. There is no proof or indication for this, for the use of an example with something does not require its existence. It has been permitted that this parable be of the type of the allegorical metaphor and comparison, and that the parable be borrowed for the strange situation, with the implied (strike) as "a parable, like two men," without comparison or metaphor. It has been stated that the two men in the parable are the polytheists of Mecca, with their pride in their wealth, their arrogance in their servants, and their scorning of the weak among the believers. And what the affair of the two groups came to, which corresponded to the parable it illustrates, corresponded in a manner that spread across the horizons, as a confirmation of His promise, Exalted is He, that the matter in the Hereafter will be higher: ﴿And the Hereafter is greater in ranks and greater in preference﴾ [al-Isra': 21].

Then Exalted is He pointed to the swift passing of what they enjoy of this world and in which they exult, with His words, Glorified is He:

The discussion on the interpretation (ta'wil) of His saying, exalted is He:

[45] ﴿And present to them the parable of the life of this world: it is like water which We send down from the sky, and the vegetation of the earth mingles with it, and then it becomes dry stalks which the winds scatter. And Allah is ever Able over all things.﴾

﴿And present to them the parable of the life of this world﴾, i.e., mention to them something that resembles it in its freshness and in how quickly it passes away: ﴿like water which We send down from the sky, and the vegetation of the earth mingles with it﴾, i.e., the plants thicken and grow dense because of it, until some of them intermingle with others, so they grow tall and lush, and blossoms, light and freshness cover them. ﴿Then it becomes﴾, i.e., after that splendor: ﴿dry stalks﴾, i.e., dry, withered and broken. ﴿which the winds scatter﴾, i.e., they disperse it and blow it away to the right and to the left, as though it had never been. Such is the condition of this world and the condition of its criminals: what they gain of the honor of life is like what the plant gains of the honor of growth, and then they pass away as the plant passes away. ﴿And Allah is ever Able over all things﴾, i.e., over both bringing into being and bringing to an end, with complete power.

Since this parable for the life of this world is among the most delightful and most striking of parables, it has been presented many times in the revelation, such as His saying, exalted is He, in Surat Yunus: ﴿Indeed, the likeness of the life of this world is like water which We send down from the sky, and the vegetation of the earth mingles with it, from which men and livestock eat﴾ [Yunus: 24]. And in az-Zumar: ﴿Have you not seen that Allah sends down water from the sky and makes it flow as springs in the earth, then brings out by it crops of varying colors﴾ [az-Zumar: 21], and so on. And in al-Hadid: ﴿Know that the life of this world is but play and amusement and adornment and boasting among yourselves and competition in wealth and children, like a rain whose plants please the disbelievers﴾ [al-Hadid: 20], and so on.

Then Allah, exalted is He, explained the status of the worldly adornments of which they used to boast, by His saying:

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[46] ﴿Wealth and children are the adornment of the worldly life, but the enduring good deeds are better with your Lord in reward and better in hope.﴾

﴿Wealth and children are the adornment of the worldly life﴾ because of their helping one in it and the honour that comes with them. Then He pointed out that they are not among the causes of honour in the Hereafter, since one has no need for them there, by His saying: ﴿but the enduring good deeds are better with your Lord in reward and better in hope﴾. That is: the deeds whose fruits remain in the Hereafter, of beliefs, morals and complete acts of worship, are better with your Lord than wealth and children, in reward and in benefit, and better than the hope attached to them. For the worldly hopes gained through them are destined to vanish, whereas what is gained through the enduring good deeds, of stations of nearness to the Lord and everlasting bliss, neither vanishes nor is changed.

Subtleties:

1 - Wealth is mentioned before children because of its prominence in what it is associated with of adornment and provision, and because the need for it is more pressing, and because it is an adornment even without them, though not vice versa.

2 - The word "adornment" (zīnah) is singular although it is predicated of the two, because it is originally a verbal noun. It is used in the sense of the thing adorned, as an intensification, as if it were the very essence of adornment. Its attribution to "the life" (al-ḥayah) is an exclusive attribution, because its adornment is specific to it.

3 - The enduring deeds and their righteousness are presented in the form of attributes that are already established, although their proper purpose is to convey information, especially in contrast with the affirmation of perishing for what corresponds to them of wealth and children, in the manner of: ﴿What is with you will be exhausted, and what is with Allah is enduring﴾ [al-Nahl: 96], to signal that their permanence is a certain matter needing no explanation. Rather, the word "al-bāqiyāt" is a name for them, not a descriptor; for this reason the modified noun is not mentioned. What needs to be addressed is their superiority.

4 - The repetition of "better" (khayr) signals the difference between the two aspects of superiority and emphasis. This is what is derived from Abu al-Su'ud, with an addition.

5 - The early scholars' tafsir of "the enduring good deeds" has been reported as prayers, deeds of Hajj, charities, fasting, jihad, manumission, the saying "Glory be to Allah, praise be to Allah, there is no god but Allah, and Allah is greatest," good speech, and other things, both traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) and stated as the words of companions. Whatever of this is traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) has not been recorded in the two Sahihs. All of it is by way of example, and the noble wording encompasses them as being among its instances.

Then Allah, exalted is He, pointed to warning the polytheists about the terrors of the Resurrection, which is the true promise and the decisive truth, by His saying, glorified is He:

The discussion concerning the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[47] ﴿And [remember] the Day We set the mountains in motion, and you see the earth laid bare, and We gather them, and We leave not one of them behind.﴾

﴿And the Day We set the mountains in motion﴾ means: remember the Day We uproot them from their places and set them moving through the air, as His saying, exalted is He, indicates: ﴿And you see the mountains, thinking them fixed, while they pass by as the clouds pass by﴾ [an-Naml: 88]. Or [it means] We set their parts in motion after We make them scattered dust: ﴿and you see the earth laid bare﴾, because what is beneath the mountains comes forth, i.e., appears, when they are blown away, and what is other than it comes forth by the removal of the mountains and the dunes, until it appears to the eye as a level plain, with no building, no tree, no landmark, and nothing else of the kind. ﴿And We gather them﴾, i.e., We assemble them at the place of standing for reckoning. ﴿And We leave not﴾, i.e., We do not leave behind, ﴿one of them﴾, i.e., neither small nor great. As He said: ﴿Say, indeed the former and the latter [generations] ﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 49] ﴿will surely be gathered to the appointed time of a known Day﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 50], and He said: ﴿That is a Day for which mankind will be gathered, and that is a Day witnessed﴾ [Hud: 103].

The discussion concerning His saying, exalted is He:

[48] ﴿And they will be presented before your Lord in rows. "You have certainly come to Us as We created you the first time. But you claimed that We would not appoint for you a appointment."﴾

﴿And they will be presented before your Lord in rows﴾ means: arrayed in ranks, ordered in their stations, none of them screening another, each in his own rank. So said al-Qashani.

Abu al-Su'ud said: (rows) means: not scattered and not mixed together. Thus there is no indication in it regarding the unity of the row or its multiplicity.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Their state is likened to the state of soldiers presented before the sultan, drawn up in rows and visible, so that he sees their group as he sees each one of them individually, and no one screens anyone else. ﴿You have certainly come to Us as We created you the first time﴾ means: without wealth and without sons. Or: "We have certainly raised you as We originated you." The speech is according to the implied "saying," i.e., "and We will say," as a rebuke to those who denied the Return and a reproach to them before the heads of the witnesses. ﴿But you claimed﴾ means: by your denial of resurrection. ﴿that We would not appoint for you an appointment﴾ means: a time for the fulfilment of what We promised you of resurrection, rising from the graves, reckoning and recompense. So they did nothing at all for that, but rather did what increased them in disgrace. And (bal, "but/rather") is for moving from one story to another; the turning is a transition, not a nullification.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 18, verse 49:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[49] ﴿And the Book will be placed, and you will see the criminals fearful of what is in it, and they will say, "Woe to us! What is this Book that leaves nothing small or great except that it has enumerated it?" And they will find what they did present. And your Lord does not wrong anyone.﴾

﴿And the Book will be placed﴾, i.e., the pages of deeds will be placed before Allah in the presence of all creation. ﴿And you will see the criminals fearful﴾, i.e., afraid that they will be exposed, ﴿of what is in it﴾, i.e., of their evil deeds that have been inscribed. ﴿And they will say, "Woe to us!"﴾, i.e., "Destruction for us and regret for us over what we neglected in our lives." Al-Qashani said: They call out for the ruin by which they were ruined, from the effect of corrupt belief and evil deeds. ﴿What is this Book that leaves nothing small or great except that it has enumerated it?﴾, i.e., what state is this? It leaves no sin, small or great, without recording and preserving it. The interrogative is figurative, expressing wonder at its enumeration of all acts of disobedience, its counting of their measures and attributes, and its not overlooking any of them.

Al-Biqa'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The particle of genitive (lam al-jarr) was written separately (meaning: in the Uthmani script), indicating that because of the intensity of distress, they pause on part of the word. This is one of his subtleties, may Allah have mercy on him. ﴿And they will find what they did present﴾, i.e., written down in detail in the pages, of good and evil. As He, exalted is He, said: ﴿The Day every soul will find what it has done of good present﴾ [Al 'Imran: 30], and He said: ﴿On that Day man will be informed of what he sent ahead and kept back﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 13].

﴿And your Lord does not wrong anyone﴾, i.e., by recording against him what he did not do, or by increasing his punishment. Then (p-4070) He, exalted is He, pointed out that disbelief and disobedience originate from obeying Satan and preferring him over the Most Merciful. Satan is the greatest of enemies and the most wicked of the wicked. None takes him as a guardian except one who has foolishly harmed himself and strayed from the right path. So He, glorified is He, said:

The Discussion of the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[50] ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," they prostrated, except Iblis. He was of the jinn, so he defied the command of his Lord. Will you then take him and his descendants as allies instead of Me, while they are an enemy to you? Wretched is the exchange for the wrongdoers.﴾

﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," they prostrated, except Iblis. He was of the jinn﴾: i.e., of the rebellious, obstinate devils. ﴿So he defied the command of his Lord﴾: i.e., he departed from His obedience. ﴿Will you then take him and his descendants as allies instead of Me, while they are an enemy to you?﴾: i.e., will you substitute them for Me, obeying them in place of obeying Me, while they are an enemy to you, seeking to bring harm upon you and leading you into ruin? This is a rebuke and reproach for those who preferred to follow and obey him. Hence Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Wretched is the exchange for the wrongdoers﴾: i.e., those who place a thing in other than its proper place. ﴿An exchange﴾: wretched is the exchange from Allah that Iblis is, for whoever substitutes him and obeys him in place of obeying Him.

Ibn Kathir said: This station is like His words, after mentioning the Resurrection, its terrors, and the final destinations of each of the two groups, the happy and the wretched, in Surah Ya-Sin: ﴿And stand apart today, O criminals﴾ [Ya-Sin: 59] up to His words: ﴿Did you not then use your reason?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 62], and His words, Exalted is He:

The discourse on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[51] ﴿I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor the creation of themselves, nor was I one who would take the misleaders as helpers.﴾

﴿I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) brought to show that Iblis and his offspring do not deserve to be taken for the purpose mentioned concerning themselves, after the explanation of the factors that turn one away from that, namely the wickedness of arrogance, transgression, and enmity. That is: I did not bring Iblis and his offspring to witness the creation of the heavens and the earth when I created them. ﴿Nor the creation of themselves﴾ means: nor did I make some of them witness the creation of others among them either. The negation of making them witness is a metonymy for the negation of seeking their support and aid in creating what has been mentioned, and it is more emphatic: for whoever has not witnessed something, how could he be sought for help in it? How could it be valid to make him a partner? For this reason, He, glorified is He, said: ﴿nor was I one who would take the misleaders as helpers﴾, that is: nor was I one who would take them as aides in creating what has been mentioned; rather, I alone created all of that without any helper or supporter. That is: if they were not a support in creation, then why do you take them as partners in worship? The deserving of worship is among the consequences of being the Creator, and associating them in it necessitates associating them in worship, while creatorship is negated from other than Him, exalted is He. So its consequence, which is the deserving of worship of that other, is negated, and they are the misleaders, so they cannot be lords. The phrase "the misleaders" (al-mudilliyn) was placed in the position of the pronoun to censure them and to record upon them the act of misleading, and to emphasize what preceded concerning the denial of taking them as allies. Similar to this verse is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Call upon those whom you claim besides God; they do not possess an atom's weight in the heavens or in the earth, and they have no share in them, nor has He any supporter among them﴾ [Saba': 22] ﴿and intercession with Him does not benefit except for one whom He permits﴾ [Saba': 23].

And His saying, exalted is He:

**The discussion on the interpretation of His, the Exalted, saying:**

[52] ﴿And [mention] the Day He will say, "Call those whom you claimed to be partners of Mine," so they will call them, but they will not respond to them, and We will place between them a place of destruction (mawbiq).﴾

﴿And the Day He will say﴾, i.e., the Truth, the Exalted: ﴿"Call those whom you claimed to be partners of Mine"﴾, i.e., in the worldly life, that they were partners who would deliver you from what you are in. This is said to them before all the witnesses, as a rebuke and reproach: ﴿so they will call them﴾, i.e., they will call upon them for help, to maintain their belief in their polytheism: ﴿but they will not respond to them﴾, i.e., they will not help them, because they are incapable of answering, let alone helping. In its mention, despite its being evident, there is mockery of them and an announcement that they are so foolish that they will not understand it except by its explicit statement. ﴿And We will place between them﴾, i.e., between the disbelievers and their gods: ﴿a place of destruction (mawbiq)﴾, i.e., a place of ruin in which they share, which is the Fire; or enmity which, in its severity, is itself destruction, like the saying of ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him: "Let your love not be excessive, nor your hatred a ruin." This is supported by the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And they have taken other than Allah as gods that they might be for them a source of honor﴾ [Maryam: 81] ﴿No! They will reject their worship of them and will be opposed to them﴾ [Maryam: 82].

Ibn Kathir said: As for if the pronoun in His saying "between them" is taken to refer to the believers and the disbelievers, as ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAmr said, that it separates the people of guidance from the people of error by it, then it is like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And on the Day the Hour will be established, that Day they will be separated﴾ [al-Rum: 14], and He said: ﴿That Day they will be divided﴾ [al-Rum: 43], and the Exalted said: ﴿And separate yourselves today, O criminals﴾ [Ya-Sin: 59], and the Exalted said: ﴿And [mention] the Day We will gather them all and then say to those who associated others with Allah, "Stay in your place, you and your partners." Then We will separate them﴾ [Yunus: 28] up to His saying: ﴿and what they used to invent will have forsaken them﴾ [Yunus: 30].

The Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on Surah 18, verse 53:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[53] ﴿And the criminals will see the Fire, and they will think that they are going to fall into it, and they will not find from it any place of turning away.﴾

﴿And the criminals will see the Fire﴾, i.e., Jahannam, encompassing every kind of destruction. The apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun to make explicit their criminality and to censure them for it. ﴿And they will think that they are going to fall into it﴾, i.e., they will be certain that they are about to fall into it. ﴿And they will not find from it any place of turning away﴾, i.e., any refuge to which they could turn. This is an indication of the distress and grief that will overtake them immediately, for the anticipation of punishment and the fear of it before its occurrence is itself an immediate punishment.

(p-4073) On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[54] ﴿And We have certainly diversified in this Qur'an for the people from every kind of example. But man has ever been, most of anything, quarrelsome.﴾

﴿And We have certainly diversified in this Qur'an for the people from every kind of example﴾ That is: We have varied, in this Qur'an which comprises the essential matters and all kinds of felicities, for the benefit and advantage of the people, from every kind of example, alerting them to the stations of felicity and the abysses of misguidance, so that they may be warned by it. ﴿But man has ever been, most of anything, quarrelsome﴾ That is: most given to disputing, contending, and opposing the truth with falsehood.

The discourse on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[55] ﴿And nothing prevented the people from believing when the guidance had come to them, and from seeking forgiveness of their Lord, except that the way of the former peoples should befall them, or that the punishment should come upon them face to face.﴾

﴿And nothing prevented the people﴾, i.e., the people of Makkah whose falsehoods have been related, and everyone who resembles them: ﴿from believing﴾, i.e., from believing in God Exalted and abandoning polytheism (shirk): ﴿when the guidance had come to them﴾, i.e., the Qur'an and the clear, luminous truth: ﴿and from seeking forgiveness of their Lord﴾, i.e., for their past sins: ﴿except that the way of the former peoples should befall them﴾, i.e., the demand for its coming, or the waiting for its coming, and it is the punishment of annihilation (ʿadhab al-isti'sal): ﴿or that the punishment should come upon them face to face﴾, i.e., they would see it with their own eyes and in direct confrontation, and it is the punishment of the Hereafter. Or it is more general. And qubul, with two dammas, carries the meaning of "with their own eyes" (ʿiyan), as in the reading (qibalan), with a kasra on the qaf and a fatha on the ba'. Or (qubulan) means: in various kinds, the plural of (qubayl), and it was read with two fathas, meaning: "in front of them" (mustaqbalan). And His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 18, verse 56:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[56] ﴿We send not the messengers except as bringers of good news and warners. And those who disbelieve dispute by means of falsehood in order to refute thereby the truth, and they take My signs and that with which they are warned in mockery.﴾

﴿We send not the messengers except as bringers of good news and warners﴾ That is: We do not send them, before the descent of the punishment, except to give good news to those who believe of nearness (to Allah) and honour, and to warn those who disbelieve, lest there come upon them the way (sunnah) of those who passed before. ﴿And those who disbelieve dispute by means of falsehood﴾ like demanding signs. ﴿in order to refute thereby the truth﴾ That is: to remove by disputation the truth that is established from its place. But that is not something that will be achieved for them. The origin of al-idhhad (refutation) is the slipping of the foot and its removal from its footing. So it is borrowed from the sensory slipping of the foot for the removal of the intelligible truth.

Al-Shihab said: You may say: in it is a comparison of their speech to a loathsome mire. Then he recited for himself:

"He brought us mire to deny it, so as to make the feet of these proofs slip."

﴿and they take My signs and that with which they are warned in mockery﴾ That is: and their warning. Or, and that with which they were warned of punishment: mockery, meaning derision and ridicule, and this is the most severe form of denial. It is described with the verbal noun for emphasis.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 18, verse 57:

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[57] ﴿And who is more unjust than one who is reminded of the signs of his Lord but turns away from them and forgets what his hands have put forth? Indeed, We have placed over their hearts coverings, lest they understand it, and in their ears deafness. And if you invite them to guidance, they will never be guided, ever.﴾

﴿And who is more unjust than one who is reminded of the signs of his Lord but turns away from them﴾ is a metaphor, in the most eloquent style, for not reflecting upon them and not taking admonition from them. ﴿And forgets what his hands have put forth﴾, i.e., what he has done of disbelief and sins, and he diverted what he was blessed with to other than that for which it was created, so he did not reflect upon the consequence of that. ﴿Indeed, We have placed over their hearts coverings lest they understand it﴾, i.e., We placed over them many veils and coverings, out of aversion to their understanding it, i.e., to their coming to know the true reality of that for which the blessings were created. ﴿And in their ears deafness﴾, i.e., We placed in them a heaviness that prevents them from listening to it. The clause is a causal explanation of their turning away and forgetting, in that they are sealed upon their hearts, because of their preference for misguidance over guidance, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate﴾ [al-Saff: 5].

﴿And if you invite them to guidance, they will never be guided, ever﴾, i.e., there will never occur from them any guidance at all.

**Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 18, verse 58:**

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[58] ﴿Your Lord is the All-Forgiving, the Possessor of mercy. Were He to seize them for what they have earned, He would hasten their punishment for them. But they have an appointed time, from which they will find no refuge other than Him.﴾

﴿Your Lord is the All-Forgiving, the Possessor of mercy. Were He to seize them for what they have earned, He would hasten their punishment for them. But they have an appointed time, from which they will find no refuge other than Him.﴾ There are many verses with this meaning, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if God were to seize people for what they have earned, He would not leave upon its back a single creature﴾ (Fatir: 45), and His saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is full of forgiveness for the people despite their wrongdoing﴾ (al-Ra'd: 6). "Your Lord" (*Rabbuka*) is the subject (*mubtada'*, the grammatical subject of a nominal sentence), and ﴿the All-Forgiving﴾ (*al-Ghafur*) is its predicate (*khabar*). The attribute of forgiveness is placed before the attribute of mercy because it is more important given the circumstances, since the context is one of explaining the delay of punishment for them after they have become deserving of it. This is indicated by His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿Were He to seize them for what they have earned﴾. The appointed time mentioned is the Day of Badr, or the conquest (*al-Fath*) referred to in many verses, or the Day of Resurrection. All of these apply to them. And (*al-Mawil*) means the refuge and the place of safety, meaning: they have no escape from Him and no way out. And His saying, exalted is He:

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

[59] ﴿And those towns — We destroyed them when they did wrong, and We appointed for their destruction an appointed time.﴾

﴿And those towns﴾ — that is, the towns of ʿAd and Thamud and their like. ﴿We destroyed them when they did wrong﴾ — through disbelief and transgression. ﴿And We appointed for their destruction an appointed time﴾ — that is, a specific time from which they had no escape. This is offered as an illustration of what He did with the Quraysh in fixing a due time [for their punishment], so that they would take heed and not be deceived by the delay of the punishment. Then the Exalted pointed to the story of Musa with al-Khidr, peace be upon them both, a story that contains benefits, wisdom and signs of prophethood that are not hidden from one who reflects. As you will see, we will touch upon fragments of it. Then He, glorified is He, said:

The discussion on the interpretation (ta'wil) of His saying, exalted is He:

[60] ﴿And when Moses said to his servant, "I will not cease until I reach the meeting place of the two seas, or I will journey on for a long time."﴾

﴿And when Moses said to his servant, "I will not cease until I reach the meeting place of the two seas, or I will journey on for a long time."﴾ That is: remember the time when Moses said to his servant, "I will not cease (la abrah)," meaning, "I will not stop travelling, until I reach the meeting place of the two seas," meaning the place where the two seas meet. "There I will find al-Khidr. Or I will travel for a long time if I do not find him there, and then I will be certain that the goal has been lost."

Al-Mahayimi said: That is: remember for those (who reject you), if you call them to guidance, they will never be guided, because of their arrogance towards you: "Indeed, you are not more knowledgeable than Moses, nor more rightly guided than him. And you are not less than al-Khidr in guidance; rather, you are greater, because your guidance is outward and inward, whereas al-Khidr's guidance is only inward. You do not need to bear hardships to attain it, whereas Moses needed it."

The term al-fata (the young man) means the youth. Al-Shihab said: The Arabs call a servant a fata, because it is generally the case that one employs someone of the age of youthful vigour. Yusha' was the servant of Moses, peace be upon him, and loved him, and was jealous for his honour. For this reason Moses singled him out as his companion and servant. He later became the successor to Moses over the Children of Israel, and God, exalted is He, granted him the conquest of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) and gave him victory over the tyrants.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 18, verse 61:

The words of His, exalted is He:

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[61] ﴿So when they reached the junction of the two seas, they forgot their fish, and it took its way into the sea, leaving a tunnel.﴾

﴿When they reached the junction of the two seas﴾, i.e., the two seas: ﴿they forgot their fish﴾, i.e., the news of their fish, and they did not check on its condition. They had taken it along as provision.

﴿It took its way﴾, i.e., its path: ﴿into the sea, leaving a tunnel﴾, i.e., like the burrow (sarab) in the earth, with a clear course, a miracle made into a sign for the one being sought.

The discussion of His words, exalted is He:

[62] ﴿So when they had passed beyond it, he said to his young man, "Bring us our morning meal; we have certainly suffered fatigue from this journey of ours."﴾

﴿So when they had passed beyond it﴾ means: beyond the meeting place of the two of them, which is the place where they had forgotten the fish. ﴿He said to his young man, "Bring us our morning meal"﴾ means: that with which we may have our midday meal. ﴿we have certainly suffered fatigue from this journey of ours﴾ means: exhaustion and hardship.

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, words:

[63] ﴿He said, "Did you see when we took refuge at the rock? Indeed, I forgot the fish, and none caused me to forget it except Satan, that I should mention it. And it took its way into the sea in a wondrous manner."﴾

﴿He said, "Did you see when we took refuge at the rock? Indeed, I forgot the fish"﴾ That is, the news of the fish. The attribution of forgetting to both of them at first is either in the sense of forgetting to seek it and being heedless of checking on it, since there was no need for it, or it is by way of *taghlib* (the rhetorical device of giving precedence to one party over another), on the basis that the one who forgot was only Yusha' (Joshua). He forgot to inform Musa (Moses) of its wondrous matter. This is like His, may He be exalted, words: ﴿From both of them come forth pearls and coral﴾ [al-Rahman: 22], whereas they come forth only from the salt water. ﴿And none caused me to forget it except Satan, that I should mention it﴾ That is, to you. "*An adhkurahu*" (that I should mention it) is a *badal* (substitution in apposition) for the pronoun in "*ansanihi*" (caused me to forget it); that is, "none caused me to forget its mention except Satan." Hafs read the *ha'* with a *damma* without the *sila* (lengthening vowel) when pausing in continuous recitation, while the rest read it with a *kasra*. ﴿And it took its way into the sea in a wondrous manner﴾ That is, a wondrous matter, since the water became a passage for it.

(p-4078)

The interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[64] ﴿He said: That is what we were seeking.﴾ So they returned, retracing their footsteps.

﴿He said﴾, i.e., Musa (Moses): ﴿That﴾, i.e., the place where the fish took its path into the sea as a way of escape: ﴿is what we were seeking﴾, i.e., we were seeking al-Khidr there, because it is the sign of the one sought. It was recited in the Seven [canonical readings] with the yā' after the ghayn (i.e., nabghī) pronounced when connected, not when stopped; with it pronounced in both states; and with it omitted in the same manner. ﴿So they returned, retracing their footsteps﴾, i.e., they went back walking, following the traces of their feet, tracking them. ﴿Retracing (qaṣaṣan)﴾, i.e., following, so that the place would not escape them a second time.

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

[65] ﴿So they found a servant from among Our servants, whom We had given mercy from Us and taught knowledge from Our presence.﴾

﴿So they found﴾ — that is, they reached the place where the fish had been forgotten. ﴿They found a servant from among Our servants﴾ — the indefinite form (ta'nir) is for magnification, and the idafah (genitive construction) in "Our servants" is for honour. The majority of scholars hold that he is al-Khidr (Khidr). We shall discuss some of his story, with God's help, after the completion of the narrative. ﴿We had given him mercy from Us﴾ — that is, We had given him a mercy from His presence (rahmah ladunniyyah), singling him out with it. ﴿And taught him knowledge from Our presence﴾ — that is, a sublime knowledge which We had preferred for him. It is a knowledge from His presence (ilm ladunni), which comes with divine support. If God, may He be exalted, wills, we shall mention the knowledge from His presence (al-ilm al-ladunni) at the end of this narrative.

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

[66] ﴿Musa said to him: "May I follow you on condition that you teach me of what you have been taught, [that which is] right guidance?"﴾

﴿Musa said to him, "May I follow you?"﴾ That is, "May I accompany you" ﴿on condition that you teach me of what you have been taught﴾ — that is, from your Lord — ﴿right guidance﴾; that is, knowledge that leads to rectitude, meaning guidance and attaining what is good.

Al-Qadi said: In this he observed the utmost humility and courtesy. He regarded himself as ignorant, asked permission to be a follower of him, and requested that he guide him and bestow favor upon him by teaching him some of what God had bestowed upon him. That is, this is how the seeker's request of the scholar ought to be.

[67–68] "He said: 'Indeed, you will not be able to have patience with me.'" "And how can you have patience about that which you do not encompass in knowledge?"

"He said: 'Indeed, you will not be able to have patience with me'" — meaning: not in any way whatsoever. Then he gave a reason for his excuse, saying: "And how can you have patience about that which you do not encompass in knowledge" — meaning: concerning matters you will see. If you accompany me, their outward appearances are objectionable (manākīr), and their inner realities are such that your knowledge does not encompass them.

[67–68] "He said: 'Indeed, you will not be able to have patience with me.'" "And how can you have patience about that which you do not encompass in knowledge?"

"He said: 'Indeed, you will not be able to have patience with me'" — meaning: not in any way whatsoever. Then he gave a reason for his excuse, saying: "And how can you have patience about that which you do not encompass in knowledge" — meaning: concerning matters you will see. If you accompany me, their outward appearances are objectionable (manākīr), and their inner realities are such that your knowledge does not encompass them.

The account of His saying, exalted is He:

[69] ﴿He said, "You will find me, God willing, patient, and I will not disobey you in any matter."﴾

﴿He said, "You will find me, God willing, patient, and I will not disobey you in any matter."﴾ That is: I will not oppose you in anything.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Musa, peace be upon him, hoped, out of his eagerness for knowledge and its increase, that he would be able to have patience with him after al-Khidr had disclosed the reality of the matter. So he promised him patience, making it conditional upon God's will, knowing the severity of the matter and its difficulty, and that the zeal which seizes the reformer when he witnesses corruption is something that cannot be borne. This is along with his knowledge that the infallible Prophet, whom God had commanded him to travel to, follow, and take knowledge from, is free from undertaking what contains a blemish in the religion. And that there must be, for what its outward appearance makes repugnant, an inward aspect that is good and beautiful. So how much more so if he did not know? End of quotation.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 18, verse 70:

(p-4080) The discussion on the interpretation of His, the Exalted, saying:

[70] ﴿He said: "If you follow me, then do not ask me about anything until I myself mention it to you."﴾

﴿He said: "If you follow me, then do not ask me about anything until I myself mention it to you."﴾ That is: do not open with questioning me about anything you find objectionable in me, and whose correct basis you do not know, until I begin to explain it to you. This is among the manners of the student with the scholar, and of the one followed with the follower.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 18, verse 71:

The discussion of His, the Exalted's, saying:

[71] ﴿So they set off until, when they boarded the ship, he made a hole in it. He said, "Have you made a hole in it to drown its people? You have certainly done a terrible thing."﴾

﴿So they set off﴾, i.e., along the shore of the sea, seeking a ship. ﴿until, when they boarded the ship, he made a hole in it. He said, "Have you made a hole in it to drown its people? You have certainly done a terrible thing"﴾, i.e., a great matter (ʿaẓīman), involving the destruction of the ship, the killing of a large group without any wrongdoing, and ingratitude for the favour of being carried without a fare.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 18, verse 72:

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

[72] ﴿He said, "Did I not tell you that you would not be able to have patience with me?"﴾.

﴿He said, "Did I not tell you that you would not be able to have patience with me?"﴾ Al-Khidr reminded him of the condition that had preceded.

That is, "This deed I did intentionally, and it is among the matters about which you stipulated with me that you would not object to me concerning them, because you have not encompassed knowledge of them, for they have a secret that you do not know."

The commentary on His words, the Exalted:

[73] ﴿He said: "Do not hold me accountable for what I forgot, and do not burden me with difficulty in my affair."﴾

﴿He said﴾, that is, Musa (Moses): ﴿"Do not hold me accountable for what I forgot"﴾ of the condition. For holding him accountable for it would lead to hardship.
