The intent is a request not to be held accountable, because of the presence of an impediment, which is forgetfulness. ﴿"And do not burden me with difficulty in my affair"﴾, that is: do not impose upon me, in acquiring knowledge from you, hardship, lest it compel me to abandon it. That is: do not make my following you difficult, but make it easy for me, by overlooking and by leaving off objection.

The discussion of His saying, exalted is He:

[74] ﴿So they set off until, when they met a boy, he killed him. [Moses] said, "Have you killed a pure soul without [its having killed] another? You have certainly done a terrible thing."﴾

﴿So they set off﴾, i.e., after they had disembarked from the ship onto the shore. ﴿until, when they met a boy, he killed him. [Moses] said, "Have you killed a pure soul without [its having killed] another"﴾, i.e., that it had not killed a soul so as to be killed. Rather, it was pure, free of the things that necessitate killing. ﴿You have certainly done a terrible thing﴾, i.e., an abhorrent thing (munkaran). Or it is more abhorrent than the first. Because that (the first act) was a breach that could be repaired by building a wall, whereas this has no way whatsoever to be repaired.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[75] ﴿He said: Did I not tell you that you would not be able to have patience with me?﴾

﴿He said: Did I not tell you that you would not be able to have patience with me?﴾ This is an emphasis in reminding him of the first condition. There is an additional subtle point in the word "laka" (to you). As al-Zamakhshari said, it adds the rebuke of direct confrontation over his rejection of the advice, and the branding with little patience at the second occurrence. This is like when a person does what you have forbidden him from, so you blame him and rebuke him, and then he does it a second time, and you increase your rebuke of him. In (al-Mathal al-Sa'ir) he said: "This is a point which the immediate consideration of the mind hardly manages to discover."

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 18, verse 76:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[76] ﴿He said, "If I ask you about anything after this, then do not keep me company. You have already received an excuse from me."﴾

﴿He said﴾, i.e., Musa: ﴿"If I ask you about anything after this"﴾, i.e., after this time: ﴿"then do not keep me company (p-4082). You have already received an excuse from me"﴾, i.e., you have found an excuse on my part, since you have given me excuse after excuse, time after time, and I have opposed you three times, in accordance with the nature of haste.

**The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:**

[77] ﴿So they set out until, when they came to the people of a town, they asked its people for food, but they refused to host them. Then they found in it a wall about to collapse, so he set it upright. He said: "If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it."﴾

﴿So they set out until, when they came to the people of a town﴾: scholars differed over the name of this town.

Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar said in *al-Fath* (*Fath al-Bari*): "The disagreement about it is like the disagreement about Majma' al-Bahrayn (the meeting place of the two seas). None of it can be relied upon."

﴿they asked its people for food, but they refused to host them﴾: that is, they refused to give them the food that was their right as guests. It is also read as ﴿يُضِيفُوهُما﴾ (yudayfuhuma), from the root *idafah* (giving hospitality). It is said: *ḍāfahu* means he came to stay with him, while *aḍāfahu* and *ḍayyafahu* mean he hosted him in his home to feed him, out of honour.

﴿they found in it a wall about to collapse﴾: that is, about to fall down soon. It is derived from *inqaḍḍa al-ṭā'ir*, meaning the bird swooped down quickly. The word "wanting" (*irādah*) is used figuratively to mean near approach and imminence, because of the lean in the wall. This is either a clear or implicit metaphor (*isti'arah*) with imaginative elements, or it is a linguistic figurative usage (*majāz lughawi mursal*) with the relation of cause (the wanting as the cause), because the fall is close.

Al-Zamakhshari, may God have mercy on him, gave many examples of this kind of figurative usage, so refer to him.

﴿so he set it upright﴾: that is, he rebuilt it and repaired it.

﴿He said: "If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it."﴾: that is, if you had asked for payment for your work so that you could be helped by it. So there is a reproach in this for leaving the wage, given how much they needed it.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 18, verse 78:

The discussion of His saying, exalted is He:

[78] ﴿He said, "This is the parting between me and you. I will inform you of the interpretation of that over which you could not have patience."﴾

﴿He said, "This is the parting between me and you."﴾ The demonstrative refers to the separation promised by his saying: ﴿So do not accompany me﴾ [al-Kahf: 76], or to the third objection, or to the present moment. ﴿I will inform you of the interpretation of that over which you could not have patience﴾ — that is, of the outcome (ma'al) and consequence (‘aqibah) of what you could not be patient with in its outward appearance. And this is: the saving of the boat from the grasp of the oppressive king; the saving of the boy's parents from his evil, together with their being granted a better substitute; and the extraction of the treasure of the two orphans. Abu al-Su'ud said: In the construction of the relative clause [in the phrase "ma lam tasti‘ 'alayhi sabran"], there is the non-ability of Musa, upon him be peace, to be patient, rather than saying "in the interpretation of what I did" or "in the interpretation of what I saw" and the like; this is a kind of indirect rebuke and reproach directed at him, upon him be peace. Then al-Khidr began to explain what had been unclear to Musa and what he had denounced in its outward appearance. Allah had revealed to al-Khidr, upon him be peace, its inner reality. So he said:

The discourse on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[79] ﴿As for the boat, it belonged to poor people who worked on the sea. I wanted to damage it, for behind them was a king who seizes every boat by force.﴾

﴿As for the boat﴾, that is, the one I made a hole in: ﴿it belonged to poor people who worked on the sea﴾, that is, to needy people who earned their living by working on the sea, carrying people from one shore to another: ﴿I wanted to damage it, for behind them was a king who seizes every boat by force﴾. That is, I only made a hole in it in order to damage it, because they would pass by him with it, and he was one of the oppressors who seizes every sound, good boat by force. So I wanted to damage it, so that he would turn away from it because of its defect.

The discussion on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[80] ﴿As for the boy, his parents were believers, and we feared that he would burden them with rebellion and disbelief.﴾ [81] ﴿So we desired that their Lord should replace him for them with one better than him in purity and nearer in compassion.﴾ [Al-Kahf: 80–81].

﴿As for the boy﴾, i.e., the one I killed: ﴿his parents were believers, and we feared﴾, i.e., had we left him: ﴿that he would burden them with rebellion and disbelief﴾, i.e., that he would bring upon them his rebellion and his disbelief and join them to it, because he had been sealed upon that. So [we] feared that he would infect them with his disease.

﴿So we desired﴾ [Al-Kahf: 81], i.e., by killing him: ﴿that their Lord should replace him for them with one better than him in purity﴾ [Al-Kahf: 81], i.e., purity from disbelief and rebellion: ﴿and nearer in compassion﴾ [Al-Kahf: 81], i.e., more compassionate toward his parents, and more dutiful.

The discussion on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[80] ﴿As for the boy, his parents were believers, and we feared that he would burden them with rebellion and disbelief.﴾ [81] ﴿So we desired that their Lord should replace him for them with one better than him in purity and nearer in compassion.﴾ [Al-Kahf: 80–81].

﴿As for the boy﴾, i.e., the one I killed: ﴿his parents were believers, and we feared﴾, i.e., had we left him: ﴿that he would burden them with rebellion and disbelief﴾, i.e., that he would bring upon them his rebellion and his disbelief and join them to it, because he had been sealed upon that. So [we] feared that he would infect them with his disease.

﴿So we desired﴾ [Al-Kahf: 81], i.e., by killing him: ﴿that their Lord should replace him for them with one better than him in purity﴾ [Al-Kahf: 81], i.e., purity from disbelief and rebellion: ﴿and nearer in compassion﴾ [Al-Kahf: 81], i.e., more compassionate toward his parents, and more dutiful.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 18, verse 82 (part 1 of 3):

(p-4084) The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:
[82] ﴿As for the wall, it belonged to two orphan boys in the city, and beneath it was a treasure belonging to them. Their father had been righteous. So your Lord desired that they should reach their maturity and extract their treasure, as a mercy from your Lord. And I did not do it of my own accord. That is the interpretation of what you could not bear with patience.﴾

﴿As for the wall, it belonged to two orphan boys in the city, and beneath it was a treasure belonging to them. Their father had been righteous. So your Lord desired that they should reach their maturity﴾ means: their strength through reason and perfection of judgment. ﴿And extract their treasure﴾ so that they may dispose of it. ﴿As a mercy from your Lord﴾ means: He bestowed it upon them as a favour.

"Mercy" (raḥmah) is an object of purpose (maf'ūl lahu), or an emphatic verbal noun (maṣdar mu'akkid) for "desired", since the desire for good is a mercy. ﴿And I did not do it﴾ means: what you saw from me. ﴿Of my own accord﴾ means: from my own effort and opinion; rather, I did it by the command of God, exalted is He. ﴿That is the interpretation of what you could not bear with patience﴾ means: of the matters that you saw; that is, its outcome and its consequence. Abu al-Su'ud said: "That" (dhālika) refers to the consequences arranged in the thread of explanation, and the sense of distance in it indicates the great elevation of their rank. And "tasṭi'" is the shortened form of "tastaṭi'", with the letter tā' deleted.

Admonitions:
Among what this narrative contains of rulings, subtleties and sublime benefits:

First: al-Suyuti said in al-Iklil: In these verses there is no harm in employing someone and taking a companion and servant on a journey; the recommendation of travelling in pursuit of knowledge; the scholar seeking more knowledge; taking provisions for a journey, and that this does not contradict reliance upon God (tawakkul); and attributing forgetting and similar disliked matters to Satan, figuratively and out of courtesy, rather than attributing them to God, exalted is He; the humility of the student towards one from whom he learns, even if that one is lower in rank; the scholar's apology to one who wishes to take from him for not teaching him what his nature cannot bear; placing the will (mashī'ah) first in a matter, and the followed party stipulating conditions upon the follower; that fulfilling conditions is obligatory; that forgetting is not a matter for which one is held accountable; (p-4085) that "for three" (li-thalāth) has consideration in repetition and the like; that there is no harm in a stranger asking for food and hospitality; that doing good is not abandoned even with miserly people; the permissibility of taking wages for work; that a poor man does not cease to be poor by owning a boat or a tool with which he earns, or something that does not suffice him; that usurpation is forbidden; that it is permissible to destroy or damage part of another's property to protect the remainder, as in the case of the trustee and the orphan; that when two harms conflict, the lesser is committed; that a child is protected by the righteousness of his father; that it is obligatory to repair what one fears may fall, and it is forbidden to neglect it until it collapses; and that it is permissible to bury wealth in the ground. End.

Al-Baydawi said: Among the benefits of this story is that a person should not be impressed by his own knowledge, nor hasten to deny what he does not approve of, for perhaps in it there is a secret he does not know; that he should persist in learning, humble himself before the teacher, and observe good manners in speech; and that he should alert the wrongdoer to his wrongdoing, and pardon him until his persistence is confirmed, and then part ways with him. End.

Among the benefits of the verse, as in Fath al-Bari: the recommendation of eagerness to meet scholars and bearing hardships for that; the application of the term "fata" (youth) to a follower, and the employment of a free man; the obedience of a servant to his master; the excuse of the one who forgets; and the permissibility of reporting fatigue, to which pain from sickness and the like is attached, provided it is not out of displeasure with what is decreed. Among them is that one who turns towards his Lord is aided, so weariness does not quickly reach him. And in it is the permissibility of seeking sustenance and seeking hospitality; that an excuse is established by the first time, and proof is established by the second time.

In it is good manners with God, and that nothing whose wording is repugnant is attributed to Him, even though all is by His decree and creation, as in the words of al-Khidr concerning the boat: ﴿So I desired to damage it﴾ [al-Kahf: 79], and concerning the wall: ﴿So your Lord desired﴾. Similar to this is his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "The good is in Your hands, and evil is not attributed to You." End.

Among its benefits is the application of the term "qaryah" (village) to "madinah" (city), by His saying: ﴿the people of a village﴾ [al-Kahf: 77], and then His saying: ﴿to two orphan boys in the city﴾.

(p-4086) Second: al-Nasir mentioned in al-Intisaf some gems from the subtleties of some of the verses mentioned, so we quote them from him.

He, may God have mercy on him, said: It is reported in a hadith that Musa, peace be upon him, did not feel fatigue, nor did he say: ﴿We have indeed met with fatigue from this journey of ours﴾ [al-Kahf: 62], except from the time he passed the place which God, exalted is He, had set as his limit. So perhaps the wisdom in causing Yusha' to forget was that Musa, peace be upon him, should become alert to the favour of God, exalted is He, upon the traveller in obedience and the pursuit of knowledge, by facilitating it for him and bearing its burdens for him. This is the continuing custom of God regarding one whose intention in an act of worship is sound: He makes it easy for him, bears its burden on his behalf, and takes charge of him as long as he remains in that state. The point of alertness is that he found a clear difference between his state during the journey toward the appointed place and his state after passing it. And God knows best. Even if Musa, peace be upon him, was alert to this, the aim is to alert others of his community, indeed of the community of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, when the story is recounted to them. God did not relate the stories of His prophets for entertainment, but so that people might exert themselves to reflect upon them and draw from their lights and benefits, in this world and the next. And God knows best.

Then he, may God have mercy on him, said: What shows that Musa, peace be upon him, was moved to hasten in denial was his zeal and fervour for the truth, for when he tore the boat he said: ﴿Have you torn it to drown its people?﴾ [al-Kahf: 71], and did not say "to drown us," thereby forgetting himself and busying himself with others, in the state in which each person says "myself, myself," not heeding wealth or children. That is the state of drowning. Glory be to Him who fashioned His prophets and chosen ones upon counselling creatures, compassion for them and tenderness toward them. May God's blessings and peace be upon them all.

Then he, may God have mercy on him, commented on the words of al-Zamakhshari: If you say that His saying: ﴿So I desired to damage it﴾ [al-Kahf: 79] is caused by fear of usurpation over it, its proper order would be to come after the cause, so why did it precede it? I say: The intention behind it is delay, and it was placed first for emphasis. Also, fear of usurpation is not the cause alone, but together with its being for the poor. It is like your saying: "Zayd, in my opinion, is staying."

He said: It is as though he made the cause of damaging it that it belonged to the poor. Then he explained the relevance of this cause to the effect, (p-4087) by mentioning the king's habit of seizing boats. This is the proper order in causal explanation: to place the judgment upon the cause, then to clarify the relevance afterward. There is no need to make it come first, and the intention is to delay it. And God knows best.

Then he said: I have contemplated, regarding the eloquence of these verses and the variation in their style, something wonderful. Do you not see that in the first he attributed the verb to his own pronoun alone, saying: ﴿So I desired to damage it﴾ [al-Kahf: 79], and in the second he attributed it to the plural pronoun, the Exalted speaking of Himself in His majesty: "So We desired that their Lord should replace them" and "so We feared that it would oppress them." Perhaps the attribution of the first to himself alone is a matter of courtesy with God, exalted is He, since what is meant is "then you damaged it," so he observed courtesy by attributing the damage to himself. As for attributing the second to the aforementioned plural pronoun, the apparent reason is that it is of the manner of the words of the king's close officials: "We ordered such-and-such, or we arranged such-and-such," while they mean: "the king ordered and arranged." This is indicated by his saying in the third: ﴿So your Lord desired that they should reach their maturity﴾. Observe how these styles vary, and do not come in one repeated pattern that the ear finds tiresome and rejects; then this variation contains the preservation of the secrets mentioned. Glory be to the Subtle, the All-Aware.

Third: al-Khafaji said: Concerning the repetition of the word "people" (ahl) here, that is, in His saying: ﴿they asked its people for food﴾ [al-Kahf: 77] following His saying: ﴿the people of a village﴾ [al-Kahf: 77], there is a well-known question. Al-Salah al-Safadi versified it, asking al-Subki about it in a poem, among which:

"I have seen the Book of God as the greatest miracle, for the best of those guided by it, of the two weighty ones,
And among the aspects of its miraculousness is that its brevity is in concise words while its meanings are expansive,
But in (al-Kahf) I saw a verse by which thought, over the length of time, has been bewildered,
And it is only ('they asked its people for food'), for we see ('they asked them for food') similar to it in clarity.
So what is the splendid wisdom in an apparent placement in place of a pronoun? Indeed that is a matter of significance."

He means that he departed from the pronoun by repeating the word "people" (ahl) and did not say "they asked it for food," because that refers to the village, nor "they asked them for food," because that refers to "people," so there must be some reason. They answered him with lengthy replies, in verse and prose. What has been established in this is that he mentioned "the people" first and it was not omitted for brevity, whether the village is taken as implied or as figuratively used, as in His saying: ﴿and ask the village﴾ [Yusuf: 82], because coming (ityan) is attributed to a place, like "I came to Arafat," and to one who is in it, like "I came to Baghdad." So had he not mentioned it, there would have been an unhelpful ambiguity. Thus what is here is not like that verse, because it is impossible to ask the village itself, so its usage is not applied in that manner. As for the second "people," it is repeated because it is other than the first. Not every definite term that is repeated is the same referent, as they have explained. For what is meant by it is some of them, since asking them one by one is unlikely. Had it not been mentioned, what is not intended would be understood. As for "they asked them," it is clear. As for "they asked it," the attribution to the place conveys comprehensiveness, as they have established in its proper place. As for the arrival of the entire village, it is literally the reaching of a part of it, as one says "Zayd is in the city" or "in the house." It has also been said that "people" is repeated for emphasis, like his saying:

"Would that the raven, on the morning it cawed between us, had been a raven with its throat cut,"

or because of the aversion to two connected pronouns coming together, due to its ugliness and length. There are other answers.

Fourth: Some of them revealed a secret for the expression first "tastaṭi'" and then finally "taṣṭi'" with the tā' deleted. He said: When al-Khidr explained to Musa and clarified for him the interpretation of what he had not borne with patience, making it plain and removing the difficulty, he said "tasṭi'" with the tā' deleted. It was said that the difficulty had been strong and heavy, so he said: ﴿I will inform you of the interpretation of what you could not bear with patience﴾ [al-Kahf: 78], matching the heavier with the heavier and the lighter with the lighter, as He said: ﴿So they could not scale it﴾ [al-Kahf: 97], which is climbing to its top, ﴿nor could they make a hole in it﴾ [al-Kahf: 97], which is harder than that. (p-4089) So He matched each with what suits it in wording and meaning. End.

Al-Shihab said: He specifically made this one with the lightened form because, since it was repeated in the story, it was fitting to lighten the last of it. As for it being to indicate that what he encountered was light upon Musa, peace be upon him, by explaining its cause, that is far-fetched, as it lies in the narration, not in what is narrated. End.

How subtle is al-Shihab's remark on such matters: "This is a flower that does not bear this rubbing."

**5th:** Imam al-Subki, may Allah have mercy on him, said: What al-Khidr, peace be upon him, did in killing the boy, because he had been created as a disbeliever, was specific to him. This is because he was inspired to act according to the inner reality, contrary to the outward appearance that accords with wisdom. So there is no difficulty in it. Yet it is known from the Shari'ah that it is not permissible to kill a child, especially between two believing parents. Even if we assume that Allah informed some of His friends, as He informed al-Khidr, peace be upon him, it would not be lawful for them to do that. As for what was narrated from Ibn Abbas (when Najda al-Haruri wrote to him: "How could he kill him when the Prophet ﷺ forbade the killing of children?" he replied: "If you know about the condition of children what the scholar of Musa knew, then you may kill"), Ibn Abbas intended by it argument and referral to what cannot be known with certainty, hoping to use the story of al-Khidr, peace be upon him, as proof. His intention was not that if that knowledge were obtained, it would be permissible, because the Shari'ah does not require it. How could one be killed for a cause that has not occurred? A newborn is not described as having true disbelief or true faith. The story of al-Khidr is to be understood as his having a independent law of his own, and he was a prophet. It was not part of the law of Musa either, which is why he (Musa) denied it. End of quotation.

Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar said in *al-Fath*: As for those who used it as evidence for permitting the averting of the greater of two harms by the lesser, that is correct, but only in matters that do not contradict an explicit text of the Shari'ah. It is not permissible to proceed to kill a person who is expected to kill many souls before he has actually committed any such act. Al-Khidr did that only because Allah, exalted is He, had informed him.

Ibn Battal said: al-Khidr's statement, "As for the boy, he was a disbeliever," refers to what his affair would have led to had he lived until he reached maturity. The permissibility of such a killing is known only to Allah. Allah may judge His creation as He wills, before puberty and after it.

I say: The import of the verse is that Musa's denial of the killing of the boy was because it was a crime without a justifying cause. That is why he said, "without a soul [to retaliate for]," and not because the boy was a child who had not reached the age of responsibility (*ḥinth*), because the verse does not indicate that. He may have been an adult. The lexicographers have said: *ghulam* means a youth who has come of age, or from birth until he grows up, and also a middle-aged man. An example of the latter is Musa's statement in the account of the Night Journey, reported from the Prophet ﷺ: "I weep because a youth was sent after me," etc. Indeed, al-Bukhari's narration may suggest that he was a child: "He found boys playing, and he took a boy and slaughtered him. Musa said: 'Have you killed a soul that has not reached the age of responsibility?'" But there is no explicit text on this, so reflect.

**6th:** Most scholars hold that the Musa mentioned in the verse is Musa son of Imran, the possessor of the famous signs and the owner of the Torah. Nawf al-Bakkali, a trustworthy Successor (*tabi'i*), who was the son of the wife of Ka'b al-Ahbar or his nephew, held that he was not Musa son of Imran, as reported in al-Bukhari. In the narration of Ibn Ishaq from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, recorded by al-Nasa'i, he said: "I was with Ibn Abbas, and with him were some people from among the People of the Book. Some of them said: 'O Abu Abbas! Nawf claims, on the authority of Ka'b al-Ahbar, that the Musa who sought knowledge was Musa son of Munnsa,' that is, son of Ifraithim son of Yusuf, peace be upon him. Ibn Abbas said: 'Did you hear that from him, O Sa'id?' I said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Nawf lied.' In al-Bukhari's narration: 'The enemy of Allah lied.' He said that only for emphasis in denying and warning against accepting his statement.

Al-Razi said: Yusuf had two sons, Ifraithim and Munnsa. The son of Ifraithim was Nun, and the son of Nun was Yusha', the companion of Musa and his successor after his death. As for the son of Munnsa, it is said that prophethood came to him before Musa son of Imran. The People of the Torah claim that he is the one who sought this knowledge in order to learn it. And al-Khidr is the one who tore the ship, killed the boy, and rebuilt the wall, while Musa son of Munnsa was with him. This is the view of the majority of the Jews. Al-Qaffal argued for the correctness of the view that he is Musa the owner of the Torah, because he is not mentioned in the Qur'an by any other description, and he is the one intended. The use of this name necessarily directs the meaning toward him. Had someone else been intended, it would have been necessary to identify him with a description that distinguishes him and removes confusion. And Allah knows best. End of quotation.

As for Ibn Abbas, his source for this, as in al-Bukhari, was what Ubayy ibn Ka'b related to him and traced to the Prophet ﷺ: "Musa was asked: 'Is there anyone on earth more knowledgeable than you?' He said: 'No.'" Or his own self suggested that to him. So Allah rebuked him for not referring the knowledge to Him, and He wanted to make him aware that among His servants on earth there is one more knowledgeable than him, so that he would not pass judgment on what he had no knowledge of. And if it is correct that Musa is the owner of the Torah, then the one meant by "his young man" is Yusha'. Musa had singled him out as a companion because of his sincerity in service, his zeal for Musa's honor, and his love for him. That is why he became his successor after him, and Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) was opened to him, and he was victorious over the tyrants, as is well known.

**7th:** Most scholars said: The companion of Musa, referred to by Allah's words, "a servant of Our servants" (Q. 18:65), is al-Khidr. They said: He was so named because whenever he sat on barren land, it turned green (*akhdara*). It is authentically reported from Ibn Abbas that he and al-Hurr ibn Qays ibn Hisn al-Fazari disputed about the companion of Musa. Ibn Abbas said: "He is al-Khidr." Then Ubayy ibn Ka'b passed by, and Ibn Abbas called him and said: "I and my companion here have disputed about the companion of Musa who sought the way to meet him. Did you hear the Messenger of Allah ﷺ mention his story?" He said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'While Musa was among an assembly of the Children of Israel, a man came to him and said: "Do you know of anyone more knowledgeable than you?" Musa said: "No." So Allah revealed to Musa: "Yes, My servant al-Khidr." Musa asked for the way to meet him, so Allah made the fish a sign for him, and it was said to him: "When you lose the fish, return, for you will meet him." Musa followed the fish's trail in the sea. Musa said: "That is what we were seeking," and they went back retracing their steps (Q. 18:64), and they found al-Khidr." And what happened between them is what Allah related in His Book."

**8th:** Scholars differed about the lineage of al-Khidr, whether he was a prophet, how long he lived, and whether his life continued, in many opinions. Some say he was a son of Adam by his own loins, or a son of Qabil (Cain), or a son of al-Yasa', or other things, all of which have no basis in knowledge. Those who said he was a prophet relied on Allah's words, "I did not do it on my own accord" (Q. 18:82), because the apparent meaning is that he did it by Allah's command, and the default is that there is no intermediary. It was said that he was a saint (*wali*). It was said that his station is below prophethood and above *siddiqiyya* (the rank of the truthful), so it is an intermediate station (*maqam barzakhi*), having one aspect toward prophethood and another toward sainthood. It was also said that he is an angel among the angels. As for his longevity, it is reported from Ibn Abbas that his lifespan was extended for al-Khidr so that he could refute the Dajjal (Antichrist).

Al-Nawawi said in *al-Tahdhib*: Most scholars said: He is alive and existing among us. This is agreed upon among the Sufis and the people of righteousness and gnosis. Their accounts of seeing him, meeting him, taking knowledge from him, asking him questions, and his presence in noble places are too numerous to count and too famous to mention.

Al-Bukhari and a group of the people of hadith said: He has died.

Al-Hafiz Abu al-Khattab ibn Dihya said: As for the report of his meeting with the Prophet ﷺ and his consoling the People of the House, nothing authentic is found through any of its chains. It is not established that he met any of the prophets except Musa. Everything reported about his being alive is not authentic, by the agreement of the transmitters. As for what comes from the shaykhs, it is strange. How can a sensible person meet a shaykh he does not know, and the shaykh says to him, "I am so-and-so," and he believes him? End of his words, summarized.

Those who held that he was long-lived relied on the story of the Spring of Life, and based it on what is mentioned of it in the Sahih of al-Bukhari and the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi. But that has not been established as a statement traced to the Prophet ﷺ.

Abu Hayyan said in his *Tafsir*: The majority hold that al-Khidr has died. Ibn Abi al-Fadl al-Mursi also held this view, because if he were alive, it would be obligatory for him to come to the Prophet ﷺ, believe in him, and follow him.

It is related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "If Musa were alive, he would have no choice but to follow me." Ibn al-Manawi, Ibrahim al-Harbi, and Abu Tahir al-Abbadi also affirmed this. Among those who affirmed that he does not exist now are Abu Ya'la al-Hanbali, Abu al-Fadl ibn Nasir, Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi, Abu Bakr ibn al-Naqqash, and Ibn al-Jawzi. Evidence was adduced for this, among it Allah's words: "We did not grant immortality to any human before you" (Q. 21:34). Abu al-Husayn ibn al-Manawi said: I searched into the longevity of al-Khidr and whether he remains alive or not. Most of the heedless people claim he is alive on the basis of what was reported about that, but the elevated (marfu') hadiths on it are weak. The chain back to the People of the Book is void because they are not reliable. The report of Maslama ibn Mishqala is like a fable, and the report of Riyah is like the wind. All the other reports are weak in both their beginnings and their ends. Their condition is one of two things: either they were inserted into reliable transmissions by deceit, or some of their transmitters deliberately fabricated them. Allah, exalted is He, said: "We did not grant immortality to any human before you" (Q. 21:34).

The author of *Fath al-Bayan* said: The truth is what we have mentioned from al-Bukhari and his peers on this matter. There is no proof in the statement of anyone, whoever he may be, except Allah, glorified is He, and His Messenger ﷺ. No definitive text or elevated hadith traced to the Prophet ﷺ has come on this, so that it may be relied upon and acted upon. The apparent meaning of the Book and the Sunnah is the negation of immortality and of long life for any human. These two are judges over others, and nothing else judges over them. Whoever says he is a prophet, a messenger, or alive and remaining has not brought a clear proof or manifest authority. When Allah's river comes, the river of Ma'qil is nullified. End of quotation.

Taqi al-Din ibn Taymiyya, may Allah's mercy and pleasure be upon him, said in one of his fatwas, concerning the appearance of jinn to humans in some lands, the following, in substance: Among the jinn are many, and they are the "men of the unseen," who are sometimes seen in these places. Allah, exalted is He, said: "And there were men among humans who sought refuge with men among jinn, so they increased them in distress" (Q. 72:6).

Likewise, those who sometimes see al-Khidr, it is a jinn they saw. Many people I know have seen him, and he said "I am..." (in some cases), and it was a jinn who deceived the Muslims who saw him. Otherwise, al-Khidr who was with Musa, peace be upon him, has died. Had he been alive during the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, he would have been obligated to come to the Prophet ﷺ, believe in him, and fight alongside him. For Allah made it obligatory on every prophet who lived to see Muhammad to believe in him and to fight alongside him, as Allah, exalted is He, said: "And when Allah took the covenant of the prophets: 'Whatever I have given you of Scripture and wisdom, then there will come to you a messenger confirming what you have, you must believe in him and support him.' He said: 'Do you affirm and accept My burden on that condition?' They said: 'We affirm.' He said: 'Then bear witness, and I am with you among the witnesses'" (Q. 3:81). Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Allah did not send any prophet without taking from him a covenant regarding his community: "If Muhammad is sent while they are alive, they must believe in him and support him." No one among the Companions reported that he saw al-Khidr, or that he came to the Prophet ﷺ. The Companions were more knowledgeable and of greater rank than to be deceived by Satan. But Satan deceived many after them, so he began to appear to one of them in the form of the Prophet and say: "I am al-Khidr." It was only Satan. Just as many people see their deceased relative come out, come to them, speak with them about matters, and fulfill needs, and they think it is the deceased himself, when it is only a devil who has taken on forms. End of quotation.

The ninth point: the words of God, exalted is He, ﴿And We taught him from Our presence a knowledge﴾ [al-Kahf: 65] indicate that there is among knowledge a hidden (ghaybi) kind of knowledge, which is called ladunni knowledge (knowledge from the presence of God). The verse is therefore the foundation for it. The proof of Islam, al-Ghazali, may God have mercy on him, composed a treatise establishing this knowledge, refuting those who denied its existence. He first mentioned some of the levels of the well-known outward sciences, and then elaborated the argument for its establishment. It is not objectionable to cite a fragment of what he established in it. He said, may God sanctify his secret: Know that human knowledge is acquired by two ways: one of them is human instruction, and the second is divine instruction.

As for the first way, human instruction, it is a known, familiar and perceptible path. It takes two forms:

One of them: from outside, which is acquisition by learning.

The other: from within, which is occupation with reflection (tafakkur). Reflection within is in the position of instruction without. For learning is the benefit a person gains from a particular person, while reflection is the benefit the soul gains from the universal soul. The universal soul is more effective and stronger in teaching than all the intellectuals and scholars. Sciences are lodged in the essence of souls potentially, like seed in the earth and a jewel at the bottom of the sea, or in the heart of a mineral. Learning is the seeking of the emergence of that which is in potential into actuality, and teaching is bringing it out from potentiality into actuality. So the soul of the learner resembles the soul of the scholar and draws near to it in relation. The scholar in conveying is like the sower, the learner in receiving is like the earth. The knowledge that is potential is like the seed, and that which is actual is like the plant. When the soul of the learner is perfected, it becomes like a fruitful tree or like a jewel appearing from the bottom of the sea. When bodily powers overcome the soul, the learner needs to increase learning over a long period, bearing the hardship of seeking benefit. When the light of intellect overcomes the qualities of sense, the seeker becomes independent through a little reflection from much learning, for the soul of the intelligent person finds in an hour of reflection benefits that the soul of the ignorant finds in a year of learning. Thus some people attain knowledge through learning and some through reflection.

Then he, may God sanctify his secret, said: The second way is divine instruction, and that is in two forms: the casting of revelation (wahy), which is the soul when it is perfected in itself, so that the filth of nature and the rust of greed and hope fall away from it. Its gaze is detached from the desires of the world, and its connection with fleeting wishes is cut. It turns its face toward its Creator and Originator, clings to the bounty of its Originator, and relies upon His bestowal and the outpouring of His light. Then God, by the goodness of His care, turns toward that soul with complete turning, looks upon it with a divine gaze, takes it as a tablet, takes the universal soul as a pen, and inscribes His sciences in it. The universal intellect becomes like the teacher and the holy soul like the student. Thus all sciences are gathered for that soul, and all forms are imprinted in it without learning or reflection.

The confirmation of this is the saying of God, Mighty and Majestic, to His Prophet ﷺ: ﴿And He taught you what you did not know﴾ [al-Nisa: 113]. The knowledge of the prophets is of the highest rank among all the knowledge of creatures, because its acquisition is from God, exalted is He, without intermediary or means. The explanation of this statement is found in the story of Adam and the angels, upon them be peace. For they, throughout their lifetimes, acquired through various methods much knowledge, until they became the most knowing of creatures and the most aware of existent things. When Adam came, he was not knowledgeable, because he had not learned nor seen a teacher. So the angels boasted over him, acted arrogantly and haughtily, and said: ﴿while we glorify You with Your praise and sanctify You﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30], and we know the realities of things. Adam returned to the door of his Creator, withdrew his heart from the totality of created things, and turned to seek help from the Lord, exalted is He. So He taught him all the names, then presented them to the angels, saying: ﴿Tell Me the names of these﴾ [al-Baqarah: 31]. Or their condition became small in Adam's presence, their knowledge diminished, and the ship of their arrogance was wrecked, so they drowned in the sea of helplessness: ﴿They said, "Exalted are You; we have no knowledge except what You have taught us"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 32]. Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿O Adam, inform them of their names﴾ [al-Baqarah: 33], and Adam informed them of the hidden treasures of knowledge and the concealed matters. Thus it is established among the intelligent that hidden knowledge arising from revelation is stronger and more perfect than acquired knowledge. The knowledge of revelation became the inheritance of the prophets and the right of the messengers, until God closed the door of revelation in the time of our master Muhammad ﷺ. So the Messenger of God was the seal of the prophets, and he was the most knowledgeable of people and the most eloquent of the Arabs and non-Arabs. He used to say: ««My Lord disciplined me and perfected my discipline»», and he said to his people: ««I am the most knowing of you about God, and the most fearful of you of God»». His knowledge was most perfect, most noble and strongest only because it was obtained from divine instruction, and he never occupied himself with human learning or teaching. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿The One of mighty powers taught him﴾ [al-Najm: 5].

The second form is inspiration (ilham). Inspiration is the alerting of the universal soul to the particular soul according to its qualities, its receptivity, its strength and its readiness. Inspiration is the effect of revelation, for revelation is the explicit statement of a hidden matter, while inspiration is its allusion. Knowledge obtained from revelation is called prophetic knowledge (ʿilm nabawi), and that obtained from inspiration is called ladunni knowledge. Ladunni knowledge is that in whose attainment there is no intermediary between the soul and the Creator. It is rather like light from the lamp of the unseen falling upon a pure, empty, subtle heart. That is because all sciences are gathered in the essence of the first universal soul, which is of the pure first separate substances, in relation to the first intellect, as the relation of Eve to Adam, upon them both be peace. It has been made clear that the universal intellect is more noble, more perfect, stronger and closer to the Creator, exalted is He, than the universal soul. The universal soul is more honoured and nobler than all other creatures. From the outpouring of the universal intellect inspiration is generated. Revelation is the adornment of the prophets, and inspiration is the ornament of the saints. Just as the soul is below the intellect, revelation is below the prophet, and likewise inspiration is below revelation. It is weak in relation to revelation, but strengthened by the addition of true dreams. Inspiration is the knowledge of the prophets and the saints. For the knowledge of revelation is specific to the messengers and restricted to them, as it was for Adam, Moses, Abraham, Muhammad and others among the messengers, may the blessings of God be upon them. He distinguished between messengerhood (risalah) and prophethood (nubuwwah). Prophethood is the receiving by the holy soul of the realities of known and intelligible things from the essence of the first intellect. Messengerhood is the conveying of those known and intelligible things to those who benefit and follow. It may happen that receiving occurs for a soul, yet conveying is not possible for it, for some excuse or cause. Ladunni knowledge belongs to the people of prophethood and sainthood, as occurred for al-Khidr, upon him be peace, when God informed us, saying: ﴿And We taught him from Our presence a knowledge﴾ [al-Kahf: 65].

Then he, may God have mercy on him, said: When God wills good for a servant, He lifts the veil between his soul and the universal soul, which is the tablet. Then some secrets of created things appear in it, and the meanings of those created things are imprinted in it. The soul then expresses them as it wills, to whomever it wills of His servants.

The reality of wisdom is attained from ladunni knowledge, and whoever has not reached this rank is not wise, for wisdom is among the gifts of God, exalted is He: ﴿He gives wisdom to whom He wills﴾ [al-Baqarah: 269] from among His servants: ﴿And whoever is given wisdom has indeed been given much good, and none will be reminded except the people of understanding﴾ [al-Baqarah: 269]. They are those who have attained the rank of ladunni knowledge, independent of abundance of acquisition and the toil of learning. They learn little and know much, and labour briefly and rest long.

Then he, may God have mercy on him, said: Know that ladunni knowledge is the diffusion of the light of inspiration, and inspiration occurs after perfection (taswiyah), as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And a soul and He who proportioned it﴾ [al-Shams: 7]. Perfection is the correction of the soul and its return to its natural disposition (fitrah). This return takes three aspects:

The first: acquiring all sciences and taking the greatest share of most of them.

The second: sincere discipline (riyadah) and correct vigilance (muraqabah). The Prophet ﷺ pointed to this truth when he said: ««Whoever acts upon what he knows, God will bequeath to him the knowledge of what he did not know»».

The third: reflection (tafakkur). When the soul has learned and been disciplined by knowledge and action, and then begins to reflect upon what it knows, under the condition of reflection, the door of the unseen opens to it, like the merchant who manages his wealth under the condition of trade, and the doors of profit open to him. If he follows the way of error, he falls into the pits of loss. The reflective person, when he follows the path of rightness, becomes one of the people of understanding, and an opening from the world of the unseen opens in his heart, so he becomes a complete, intelligent, inspired, supported scholar. As the Prophet ﷺ said: ««An hour's reflection is better than seventy years of worship»». End of the summary.

Within the course of his words, may God have mercy on him, are sentences of Sufi allusions and expressions. Sound intellect does not reject them, nor do the rules of the outward sciences, for in this position they are at the degree of moderation and balance. Thus was his path, may God sanctify his secret. And His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 18, verse 83:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[83] ﴿They ask you about Dhu al-Qarnayn. Say, "I will recite to you about him a remembrance."﴾

﴿They ask you about Dhu al-Qarnayn﴾ — he is Alexander the Great, the Macedonian (al-Iskandar al-Kabir al-Maqduni). We will mention the reason he was given this epithet. ﴿Say, "I will recite to you about him a remembrance"﴾ — that is, a report worthy of mention, a miraculous one, which Allah sent down to me.

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

[84] ﴿Indeed, We established him in the land and gave him from every thing a means.﴾

﴿Indeed, We established him in the land﴾ means: with power, opinion, and management, abundance of wealth, reinforcement through numbers, great renown, and widespread fame. ﴿And We gave him from every thing a means﴾ means: a way (ṭarīq) leading him to it. A sabab (means, cause) is that by which one reaches the desired goal, whether by knowledge, capability, or an instrument.

The discussion of God's words:

[85] ﴿So he followed a course⁠﴾ [86] ﴿until, when he reached the setting-place of the sun, he found it setting in a spring of murky water, and he found near it a people. We said, "O Dhul-Qarnayn, either punish them or treat them with kindness."⁠﴾ [Al-Kahf: 86].

﴿So he followed a course﴾ is read with a hamza of qat' (fa-atba'a, with the hamza pronounced and the ta' sukun) and also with a hamza of wasl and a shaddah on the ta' (fa-ttaba'a). It is said that both have the same meaning and both take one object. It is also said that atba'a with qat' takes two objects, and the sense is: "he followed a cause, another cause," or "he followed his affair with a cause," like His words: ﴿And We made a curse follow them in this world⁠﴾ [al-Qasas: 42].

(p-4100) Abu 'Ubayda said: ittaba'a with wasl means to travel along a route, while atba'a with qat' means to overtake, as in His words: ﴿but a piercing flame pursued him⁠﴾ [al-Saffat: 10]. Yunus said: atba'a with qat' denotes earnest diligence in the pursuit, and with wasl it denotes mere movement. The fa' in His words ﴿So he followed⁠﴾ is the fa' of al-Fasihah (the fa' that indicates an implied elision), meaning: he intended to reach the west, ﴿so he followed⁠﴾ a cause that would bring him there, consistent with His words: ﴿until, when he reached the setting-place of the sun⁠﴾ [al-Kahf: 86], i.e., the furthest point of land he traversed toward the west, which is the western extremity of the earth. ﴿He found it setting in a spring of murky water⁠﴾ [al-Kahf: 86], i.e., possessing hama' (black mud), which is black clay. It is also read as ḥāmiyah, i.e., hot, and it may comprise both attributes. And wajada (found) here may mean "saw," as al-Raghib mentioned. ﴿And he found near it a people⁠﴾ [al-Kahf: 86], i.e., a nation. Then God, exalted is He, indicated that He empowered him over them, gave him victory over them, made him their judge, and granted him the choice concerning their affair, by His words: ﴿We said, "O Dhul-Qarnayn, either punish⁠﴾ [al-Kahf: 86], i.e., by killing or otherwise, ﴿or treat them with kindness⁠﴾ [al-Kahf: 86], i.e., by pardon.

Then He, exalted is He, made clear His justice and fairness, so that His way might be followed, by His saying:

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[87] ﴿He said, "As for one who wrongs, we will torment him; then he will be returned to his Lord, and He will torment him with a terrible torment."﴾

﴿He said, "As for one who wrongs"﴾ i.e., by transgression and corruption on the earth, through polytheism (shirk), misguidance, and leading others astray: ﴿"we will torment him; then he will be returned to his Lord"﴾ i.e., in the Hereafter: ﴿"and He will torment him with a terrible torment"﴾ i.e., a dreadful punishment such as has never been known before.

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[88] ﴿As for him who believes and does righteous deeds, he shall have a reward, the best (al-husna), and We shall speak to him of Our command with ease.﴾

﴿As for him who believes and does righteous deeds, then for him﴾ i.e., in both abodes: ﴿a reward, the best (al-husna)﴾. It is read with the nominative (raf') and the genitive construction (idafa). Here it is a subject (mubtada'), or it is nominative by the adverbial phrase (al-zarf), i.e., "then for him is the reward of the best quality (al-khaslah al-husna)." It is read with the nominative and tanwin, with "al-husna" as an apposition (badal) or as the predicate of a deleted subject (khabar mubtada' mahdhuf). It is read with the accusative and tanwin, i.e., "then for him is al-husna as a reward." Thus it is a verbal noun (masdar) in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (hal), i.e., "being rewarded with it." Or it is a verbal noun in meaning, i.e., "He rewards with it a reward," or it is a specification (tamyiz). It is read with the accusative without tanwin, and it is like the tanwin reading, except that the tanwin has been dropped because of the meeting of two unvocalized letters (iltiqa' al-sakinayn). This was related by Abu al-Baqa'.

Discourse on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

﴿Then he followed a way﴾, i.e., a road returning from the setting-place of the sun, leading to its rising-place.

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, Exalted is He:

[91] ﴿Thus. And We had full knowledge of what was with him.﴾

﴿Thus﴾ means: the matter of Dhul-Qarnayn is as We have described it, in the loftiness of his position and the breadth of his dominion. Or, his affair among them is like his affair among the people of the west, in the judgment mentioned earlier. Or, it is an adjective of a verbal noun omitted from (wajada), meaning: he found it rising, a finding like his finding it setting in a muddy spring. Or, it is an object of (balagha), meaning: he reached its setting just as he reached its rising, and no one but God can comprehend what he endured. Or, it is an adjective of (qawm), meaning: over a people like that tribe over whom the sun sets, in disbelief and in judgment. ﴿And We had full knowledge of what was with him﴾, that is, knowledge. We are aware of all his circumstances and the circumstances of his army. Nothing of them is hidden from Us, even if their nations are scattered and the earth cuts them off from one another. In concluding with this, there is an indication of the great number of his troops and equipment, such that none can encompass them except His knowledge, Exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 18, verses 94–95:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[94] ﴿They said, "O Dhul-Qarnayn, indeed Gog and Magog are corrupters in the land, so shall we pay you a tribute on condition that you build between us and them a barrier?"﴾ [95] ﴿He said, "That in which my Lord has established me is better, so assist me with strength; I will make between you and them a dam.﴾ [Al-Kahf: 94–95]

﴿They said, "O Dhul-Qarnayn, indeed Gog and Magog are corrupters in the land﴾, i.e., in our land, through killing and harm. ﴿So shall we pay you a tribute﴾, i.e., a payment that we would bring out from our wealth. It has also been read as "kharaj" (خَراجًا), which has the same meaning. ﴿On condition that you build between us and them a barrier﴾, i.e., a barrier that prevents their coming out against us.

﴿He said, "That in which my Lord has established me is better﴾ [Al-Kahf: 95], i.e., that in which He has made me firmly established of wealth and dominion is greater than what you wish to give me, so I have no need of it. ﴿So assist me with strength﴾ [Al-Kahf: 95], i.e., with workers, craftsmen and tools. ﴿I will make between you and them a dam﴾ [Al-Kahf: 95], i.e., a strong barrier. The original meaning of "radm" (رَدْم, dam) is filling a breach with stones and the like.

[94] ﴿They said, "O Dhul-Qarnayn, indeed Gog and Magog are corrupters in the land, so shall we pay you a tribute on condition that you build between us and them a barrier?"﴾ [95] ﴿He said, "That in which my Lord has established me is better, so assist me with strength; I will make between you and them a dam.﴾ [Al-Kahf: 94–95]

﴿They said, "O Dhul-Qarnayn, indeed Gog and Magog are corrupters in the land﴾, i.e., in our land, through killing and harm. ﴿So shall we pay you a tribute﴾, i.e., a payment that we would bring out from our wealth. It has also been read as "kharaj" (خَراجًا), which has the same meaning. ﴿On condition that you build between us and them a barrier﴾, i.e., a barrier that prevents their coming out against us.

﴿He said, "That in which my Lord has established me is better﴾ [Al-Kahf: 95], i.e., that in which He has made me firmly established of wealth and dominion is greater than what you wish to give me, so I have no need of it. ﴿So assist me with strength﴾ [Al-Kahf: 95], i.e., with workers, craftsmen and tools. ﴿I will make between you and them a dam﴾ [Al-Kahf: 95], i.e., a strong barrier. The original meaning of "radm" (رَدْم, dam) is filling a breach with stones and the like.

**Discussion on the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:**

[96] ﴿"Bring me blocks of iron," until when he had leveled between the two cliffs, he said, "Blow," until when he had made it fire, he said, "Bring me molten copper to pour over it."﴾ [97] ﴿So they were not able to scale it, nor were they able to pierce it.﴾ [Al-Kahf: 97] [98] ﴿He said, "This is a mercy from my Lord. But when the promise of my Lord comes, He will make it level ground, and the promise of my Lord is always true."﴾ [Al-Kahf: 98].

﴿"Bring me blocks of iron"﴾, i.e., hand me its pieces. ﴿"until when he had leveled between the two cliffs"﴾, i.e., between the two sides of the two mountains. ﴿"he said, 'Blow'"﴾, i.e., into the bellows and the iron. ﴿"until when he had made it"﴾, i.e., the thing blown into, ﴿"fire"﴾, i.e., like fire by heating. ﴿"he said, 'Bring me molten copper to pour over it'"﴾, i.e., melted copper, so that it would adhere to the iron, and the structure would be strengthened and made firm with it.

﴿"So they were not able to scale it"﴾ [Al-Kahf: 97], i.e., to climb over it, because of its height and smoothness. ﴿"nor were they able to pierce it"﴾ [Al-Kahf: 97], because of its thickness and hardness.

﴿"He said, 'This'"﴾ [Al-Kahf: 98], i.e., the barrier, ﴿"is a mercy from my Lord"﴾ [Al-Kahf: 98], toward those who dwell near it, since they were safe from the evil of those whom it barred from them, and a mercy toward others, since it blocked the way to them. ﴿"But when the promise of my Lord comes"﴾ [Al-Kahf: 98], by its crumbling and ruin, ﴿"He will make it level ground"﴾ [Al-Kahf: 98], with the long vowel (dakkā'), i.e., level land. It was also read as "dakkan," meaning crushed and leveled with the ground. ﴿"and the promise of my Lord is always true"﴾ [Al-Kahf: 98], i.e., it will certainly come to pass. This is the end of the account of the words of Dhu al-Qarnayn.

**Notes:**

**The first:** We have previously stated that there is nothing of history in the Qur'an insofar as it is story and reports. Rather, what is there are signs, lessons, rulings and moral teachings manifested within the context of events. For this reason, attention must be directed to the aspects of those benefits and fruits, and to what may be derived from those verses. The account of Dhu al-Qarnayn, Alexander, has pointed to many benefits. We mention what has been opened to us from them, and we leave what we have not comprehended to the All-Knowing, the All-Aware.

(p-4104) Among its benefits: taking heed of God raising some people above others in ranks, and granting provision to whom He wills without reckoning, in dominion and wealth, because of His hidden wisdom and overwhelming power. There is no god but Him.

Among them: the indication of undertaking the means and following the sunnah (way) of God in the cosmos through diligence and work. That according to the measure of effort exerted, success and victory come. For what was related of Alexander regarding his traveling across the earth to the west and east of the sun and its rising and its north, his not slackening, his finding pleasure in continuing journeys and braving dangers, and climbing rugged terrain and seas, and then his attaining that glory which no dust can rival, is a greater lesson for people of insight.

Among them: stirring up determination to remove obstacles, and that when the means are available, one should not consider riding the sea or crossing the desert an excuse for idleness and contentment with the lowly. Rather, one should be energized and imagine, through its bitterness, the sweetness of its outcome of rest and comfort. Just as Alexander spent his life and tasted only the sweetness of triumph and the pleasure of victory, for he was not among those whom hardships keep from attaining what they seek.

Among them: the obligation to hasten toward lofty matters in youth, for it is an error to postpone them until old age. Alexander, when he assumed his father's kingdom, was around twenty years old. He undertook what he undertook in the prime of youth and the strength of vitality. He attacked the greatest kings of his era and their largest armies, as if he were decreed destiny. No number or equipment stood before him. He plunged into the torrents of destruction, neither fearful nor timid. He added the entire Eastern world to the Greek kingdom while still young. He died at the age of thirty-three, as the historians who investigated it recorded.

Among them: that whoever is able over his enemies and has power over them should not be intoxicated by the pleasure of authority, driving them with the rod of humiliation and making them swallow the bitterness of enslavement and punishment. Rather, he should treat the good with his goodness and the wrongdoer according to the measure of his wrongdoing. For what is related of Alexander, his saying: ﴿"As for the one who does wrong"﴾ [Al-Kahf: 87], to the end, is the pinnacle of justice and the utmost of fairness.

(p-4105) Among them: that the king, when injustice from neighbors is complained of to him, must exert his utmost effort for comfort and security, defending the beloved homeland and safeguarding freedom and civilization from the claws of savagery and ruin, fulfilling the duty of repelling aggressors and enforcing justice among all peoples. Just as Alexander answered the call of those who complained by building the barrier. The historians have unanimously agreed that he built several fortresses and walls to repel the raids of the barbarians and to stop their assaults.

Among them: that the king should abstain from the wealth of his subjects and renounce taking payment in exchange for work he performs, when God has made him independent of it. In this lies the preservation of his dignity and the increase of love for him. Just as Alexander refused it out of generosity and nobility.

Among them: speaking of God's blessing when the situation calls for it, like Alexander's saying in the context of his abstention from their wealth and his compassion for them: ﴿"What my Lord has established me in is better"﴾ [Al-Kahf: 95], like the saying of Solomon: ﴿"What God has given me is better than what He has given you"﴾ [An-Naml: 36]. It has been said that Alexander's revenue from the lands he conquered was about sixty million English pounds.

Among them: reinforcing walls and fortresses at the frontiers, and strengthening them with molten lead and by placing sheets of copper between solid rocks, sincerely and earnestly in the work, so that it may benefit from it across generations, for a building that is not firm yields no fruit.

Among them: the king sharing in the labor with the workers and working alongside them himself when the situation requires, to energize their task, to embolden them, and to refresh their hearts. Alexander used to share the toil with the workers and manage the work himself, as the Wise Reminder explained in His saying: ﴿"Bring me, I will pour over it molten copper."﴾

Among them: making others aware of the fruit of important work, so that they will recognize its value and show gratitude. For this reason he said: ﴿"This is a mercy from my Lord"﴾ [Al-Kahf: 98].

(p-4106) Among them: informing of the hereafter's stage and the ending of this first stage, so that souls remain yearning for that eternal world and everlasting bliss. For this reason He said: ﴿"But when the promise of my Lord comes"﴾ [Al-Kahf: 98].

Among them: taking heed of the immortalizing of noble praise and lofty legacies. For whoever reflects carefully on what is related of him in these noble verses will clearly see the excellence of his qualities and the sublimity of his virtues: courage, loftiness of aspiration, chastity, and justice. And his constant effort to establish security, to reward the good, and to discipline the wrongdoers, and his kindness to humankind, especially in an age when most of the customs and morals of both civilized and uncivilized nations were savage and corrupt.

Among them: concern for unifying the word for one who rules over diverse peoples, as Alexander's endeavor aimed at. For he strove to unify the word among the peoples and to blend these different nations so as to bind them with bonds of love and customs. It has been related that he used to muster from every nation he conquered a mighty army, adding it to his Macedonian Greek army, and he ordered his men to marry from their daughters, to strengthen the bonds of love and connection and to remove hatred and rancor.

Among them: taking heed of what a human being can attain and the lofty potential within him. It is necessary for a person first to live as a nursing infant, who knows nothing of what is around him and seeks nothing but what his weak nature needs, for the sake of what the requirements of life demand, while he is then lying helpless with no will, prone to illnesses that make him taste pain, and the cup of death may have been forced upon him before he sees or comprehends anything of this order. Then, when the forces of life prevail over the causes of death, and the strength of youth flows through his body, and he directs what God has bestowed upon him toward that for which he was created, he grows into a great person, victorious in attaining the goal of his hopes.

**The second note:** Concerning Dhu al-Qarnayn. The researchers agree that his name is Alexander son of Philip. Ibn al-Qayyim said in *Ighathat al-Lahfan*, in discussing the philosophers: "Among their kings is Alexander the Macedonian, who is the son of Philip, and he is not Alexander Dhu al-Qarnayn whose account God, Exalted is He, related in the Qur'an. Rather, between them there are many centuries, and in religion there is the greatest contrast between them.

Dhu al-Qarnayn was a righteous man who believed in God Almighty, His angels, His books, His messengers, and the Last Day. He used to fight the worshippers of idols, and he reached the eastern and western extremities of the earth. He built the barrier between the people and Gog and Magog. As for this Macedonian, he was a polytheist who worshipped idols, he and the people of his kingdom. Between him and the Messiah were about 1,600 years, and the Christians date their history from him.

Aristotle was his minister, and he was a polytheist who worshipped idols." End of his words.

There is something to consider in this. The reference in this matter is the leading historians, who have unanimously agreed that he was Alexander the Great son of Philip, founder of Alexandria, 954 years before the Hijrah, and 332 years before the birth of Jesus, peace be upon him. This has become one of the fundamental facts among geographers. As for the claim that he was a polytheist who worshipped idols, it is not accepted, even though his people were idolaters, because he was a student of Aristotle. It is mentioned in his biography, as in *Tabaqat al-Atibba'* and other works, that he did not venerate the idols that were worshipped at that time, and that because of this he was accused of disbelief and efforts were made to report him to the king. When he sensed this, he departed from Athens, for he disliked that its people be tested with what they had tested Socrates, the teacher of Plato, with. For Socrates was among their worshippers and devotees. He openly opposed them in worshipping idols, and he confronted their leaders with proofs and arguments against the falsehood of worshipping them. So the common people rose up against him and compelled the king to kill him. He then imprisoned him to restrain them from him. Then the polytheists would not be satisfied except with his killing, so he gave him poison out of fear of their evil, after long debates that took place between him and them, as recorded in *Tabaqat al-Atibba' wa Tarajim al-Falasifa*. Thus, polytheism, though it was the religion of the Greeks and the belief of their people, does not preclude that the king and his inner circle hold another belief, which they openly declare or conceal, like the Negus, king of Abyssinia, who openly professed faith in the Prophet (ﷺ), while his people and all the people of his kingdom were Christians. Likewise were Alexander, his teacher, and the sages before him. For whoever examines their biographies closely finds that they held to monotheism and belief in the Return. The judge Sa'id said: "Pythagoras, the teacher of Socrates, used to say that the soul persists and exists after death, in reward or punishment, according to the view of the divine sages." So reflect on his words "according to the view of the divine sages," and the point we have mentioned will be confirmed.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 18, verses 96–98 (part 2 of 3):

As for the statement of al-Fakhr al-Razi: "There is a strong difficulty in Alexander being Dhu al-Qarnayn. He was a pupil of the sage Aristotle (Aristatalis) and followed his doctrine, so Allah's praise of him requires the judgment that Aristotle's doctrine is true and correct. That is something there is no way to accept, so the rejection of this implication is evident." The answer is that whoever follows a doctrine and is praised for some matter that warrants his praise, it does not follow that the praise is for the sake of his doctrine and the one he follows. He may possess qualities and virtues that are not found in the one he follows, and sound insights may appear to him that are not in the doctrine in which he grew up as an imitator (muqallid). Is it not possible that he was free in his thinking, rejecting blind imitation and embracing the truth? And whoever Allah gave such dominion as He gave him, is it impossible that He would grant him, from the furnace of thought, freedom of conscience, and penetration of insight, that by which he differs from the one he follows? This is on the assumption that the one he follows is blameworthy. You already know that his teacher, meaning Aristotle, was a monotheist (muwahhid), and this is well known in history with no concealment. Moreover, even if the verse implied praise of his teacher's doctrine, that would be in the fundamental principles (usul), which are the intended matters in themselves, and these two suffice as perfection. Al-Razi has an aim by which he seizes the opportunity to honor the sages and to introduce their doctrine, and this is one of them, although he, may Allah forgive him, has dyed it in this style. Whoever knows, knows this.

The third admonition: It has been disputed what the reason is for his being titled Dhu al-Qarnayn. It was said: because he traversed the two horns of the world, meaning its two sides, east and west. Or because he had two horns, meaning two braids. Or because he ruled the Romans and Persians.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also possible that he was given this title for his bravery, just as a brave man is called a ram (kabsh) because he butts his opponents."

I say: this title is an allusion to everyone who has strength, might, and dominion, because of the horned animals, the strongest and most powerful of them. The use of "horn" as an allusion to strength and dominion is well known among the Jews, who are the questioners, and it occurs in their Tawrah (the Torah) in the prophecy of Daniel, peace be upon him, the statement about the king: "Then behold, a ram standing before the river, and it had two horns." Then his statement: "And as I was considering, behold, a male goat came from the west across the face of the whole earth, and the goat had a remarkable horn between its eyes." They said: the horn here is a symbol of strength and dominion, and the goat is a symbol of the kingdom of the Greeks, and its horn is a symbol of the first king of this kingdom, who is Alexander the Great. What it indicates about the goat's swiftness of movement is a hint at the abundance of the constant raids that struck the lands. The phrase "came from the west" points to his departure from Macedonia, which is to the west of Persia, when he advanced against the armies of Darius and defeated him, and then pursued him into the interior of his kingdom. The point is that this title "Dhu al-Qarnayn" is famous and is not peculiar to the Arabs, as some claim. Rather, it is known among the Hebrews as well, and it may appear that it is one of their particular symbols which spread to the Arabs, and they accepted it.

The fourth admonition: Al-Razi said: "They differed concerning Dhu al-Qarnayn: was he one of the prophets or not? Some said he was a prophet and argued for this with several points:
First: His statement: 'Indeed, We established him in the land,' and it is better to understand it as establishment in religion, and full establishment in religion is prophethood.
Second: His statement: '[And] We gave him of everything a way (sabab)' (18:84), and among the things is prophethood. So the generality in His statement, 'We gave him of everything a way,' requires that He gave him a way to prophethood.
Third: His exalted statement: 'We said, O Dhu al-Qarnayn, either punish them or adopt among them goodness' (18:86), and the one whom Allah addresses must be a prophet.
Others said he was a righteous servant and not a prophet." End of quote.
Then al-Razi said afterward: "His exalted statement, 'We said, O Dhu al-Qarnayn' (18:86), indicates that He spoke with him without intermediary, and this indicates that he was a prophet. If this expression is taken to mean that He addressed him through the tongues of some prophets, then that is a departure from the apparent meaning." End of quote.

It is not hidden that the argument from these proofs for his prophethood is weak, because establishing it requires explicit textual evidence and specification. As for pursuing general expressions in depth to derive such a conclusion, it is not convincing.

As for His exalted statement, "We said, O Dhu al-Qarnayn" (18:86), we have previously mentioned that it is an allusion to His establishing him over them, not a statement of direct address. Otherwise, if it were so, he would have been given the choice by Him and taught what to do with them, and then how would it be permissible for him to override that by another independent judgment? It cannot be said that the default in an unqualified usage is its literal meaning, because we say so as long as there is no preventing factor, such as what we have mentioned. The Noble Revelation has a particular style, known to whoever has deeply reflected on its wondrous exposition. Yes, if the intended meaning of those who say he was a prophet were that he was one of the inspired (mulhamin), going in the prophethood to the more general meaning that includes revelation with a law and inspiration, that would be closer to the truth. Then his prophethood would belong to the second category, which is inspiration. The Sufis apply the term to such occurrences (al-warid). It is reported in the Hadith that his companion is called muhaddath (one spoken to by inspiration), and the application of prophethood to him, although forbidden in Islam, was known before it among the righteous servants.

The fifth admonition: It was related concerning His exalted statement, "They ask you about Dhu al-Qarnayn" (18:83), two opinions as to whether the questioners were the Jews or others. The first was preferred for two reasons:
The first of them: Alexander had standing and esteem among the Jews. This is because it is related that when he conquered Gaza and approached Jerusalem (Bayt al-Maqdis), the chief of its rabbis (ahbar) came out to him and offered submission. So Alexander entered it, heard the prophecy of the Tawrah, was pleased, and treated the Jews well. Some historians criticized this report, saying it is not transmitted in Greek books, and none of their historians narrated it.
The second of them: The title "Dhu al-Qarnayn" is among the symbols of the Israelites, as we have mentioned from them previously.

The sixth admonition: They said the intended meaning of "a spring of black mud" (ʿayn ḥami'a) is the Ocean (al-Bahr al-Muhit). Its being called a spring is because, relative to the greatness of His power, exalted is He, it is like a drop, even though it is great in our estimation. They said: he saw the sun setting in its sight, sinking into the sea. This is the case for everyone who reaches its shore; they see it as if it sets in it, while it never leaves its orbit.

Imam Ibn Hazm, may Allah have mercy on him, has another opinion on the verse. He mentioned it in the book al-Milal (Kitab al-Milal), in the discussion of the sphericity of the earth. He said: "Dhu al-Qarnayn was at the spring, the hot one of black mud, as you say, 'I saw you in the sea,' meaning that when you saw it, you were in the sea. The proof of this is that the setting place of the sun is not ignored by anyone except an ignorant person, and the extent between the first of its winter setting, when it is at the end of the head of Capricorn, to the last of its summer setting, when it is at the head of Cancer, is visible and observed. Its measure is forty-eight degrees of the celestial sphere. It corresponds on the earth as a whole, by geometric proof, to less than a sixth of its measure, amounting to about three thousand miles and more. This extent cannot be called in the language 'a spring' at all, especially 'a spring of black mud' that is hot. We were addressed in the Arabic language. Since we are certain that it is a spring by the information of Allah, mighty and majestic, the Truthful, to whom falsehood does not come from before it or behind it, we know with certainty that Dhu al-Qarnayn's journey ended, in the direction he walked, at the said spring from the west, and the possibility of walking beyond it ceased for him due to the seas that blocked him there. We also know by necessity that Dhu al-Qarnayn and other people occupy no more of the earth than the area of their bodies, whether standing, sitting, or lying down. One with such a description cannot see from the earth the whole extent of the places of sunset, if its setting were in a spring of the earth, as the ignorant suppose. His line of sight must meet the earth's convexity and rises of its elevations that block the line from continuing, unless someone says that spring is the sea. Then the sea cannot be called in the language 'a spring of black mud' nor 'hot.' Allah, mighty and majestic, has informed that the sun swims in the celestial sphere and that it is only a lamp from the sphere. Allah's statement is the truth that does not contradict itself. So if it had set in a spring of the earth, as the ignorant suppose, or in the sea, the sun would have departed from the sky and left the celestial sphere, and that is falsehood. Thus it is established with certainty, without doubt, that Dhu al-Qarnayn was at the hot spring of black mud when he reached the furthest land in the west, especially given what proof has established, that the body of the sun is greater than the body of the earth. And there is another decisive proof, which is His exalted statement: 'He found it setting in a spring of black mud, and found near it a people' (18:86). So it is necessarily established that he found the people by the spring, not by the sun." End of Ibn Hazm's words.
